units.la: MDXCIII.
AD ILLVSTREM ET INCLYTVM DOMINVM, D. ALBERTVM Co-mitem in Hanavv & Rinnegk, Do-minum in Mintzenberg.
units.tr: TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS AND RENOWNED LORD, LORD ALBERT, Count of Hanau and Rinnegk, Lord of Münzenberg.

units.la: OMNIBVS incumbit fidei confeßio verę, Munia in hoc mundo qualiacunq; gerant. Sive Magistratus hi sint, cives q; gubernent, Christiadum pascant sive docendo gregem.
units.tr: Every person is bound to confess the true faith, whatever duties they perform in this world.

units.la: Sive colant artes alias: doctive rudésve: Qui sunt in Christo, sunt velut unus homo. Inprimis autem perspecta ea dogmata sunto, Quæ fundamentum religionis habent.
units.tr: Whether they are magistrates who govern the citizens, or those who feed the flock of Christians or teach it, or whether they cultivate other arts, whether learned or unlearned: those who are in Christ are like one man. Above all, the doctrines that form the foundation of religion must be thoroughly understood.

units.la: Et quæ Romanus tentat subvertere præsul, Qui sævi Satanæ vimq; vicesq; gerit. Quale est de CHRISTI VERBO, quod sufficienter Tradit Apostolicus fatidicusq; Canon.
units.tr: And those which the Roman prelate tries to overthrow, he who bears the power and the office of cruel Satan. Such is the doctrine concerning the Word of Christ, which the apostolic and prophetic canon hands down as sufficient.

units.la: Hoc Papa impugnat, nobisq; imponere gestit Traditionum ingens barbaricumq; jugum. Contra hoc pugnamus, Thesibusq; renitimur istis, Quas omnes Codex approbat ille sacer.
units.tr: The Pope attacks this and eagerly seeks to impose on us the huge and barbarous yoke of traditions. Against this we fight, and we stand firm with these theses, which that holy book approves in full.

units.la: Inscriptasq; tibi, COMES INCLYTE, mente benigna Suscipe, sint tenues exiguæq; licet: Ad Christi laudem faciunt tamen, atq; tuentur Dogmata quæ in nostris sunt celebrata Scholis.
units.tr: To you, illustrious count, I dedicate these lines; receive them with a kindly mind, though they are slight and meagre. Nevertheless they serve the praise of Christ and defend the doctrines that have been taught in our schools.

units.la: Perge, COMES GENEROSE, Deoq; bonisq; probari, Inq; tuo, CHRISTI, pectore, crescat amor. Qui CHRISTVM IESVM rectè cognoscit amatq;, Ille tenet veræ prosperitatis iter.
units.tr: Go on, noble count, and be approved by God and by good men, and may the love of Christ grow in your heart. He who rightly knows and loves Jesus Christ holds the path of true prosperity.

units.la: Amandus Polanus á Polansdorf S. Theologiæ D.
units.tr: Amandus Polanus à Polansdorf, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

units.la: DE TRADITIONIBUS.
units.tr: ON TRADITIONS.

units.la: In proximis sex disputationibus de verbo Dei σωτ-ἐιβάπ[?]μος[?]: quibus conjuncta est controversia de Traditionibus, de quibus jam, σὺν Θεῷ, acturi sumus: & quidem ita, ut primò de iis in genere, deinde in specie de Papisticis traditionibus tractemus.
units.tr: In the six preceding disputations concerning the Word of God, God willing, we are about to treat the controversy about traditions, which is connected with them. We shall do so in such a way that we first deal with traditions in general and then, in particular, with Papistical traditions.

units.la: THESIS I.
units.tr: THESIS I.

units.la: TRADITIO,(ut in Ecclesia hoc nomine utimur) est quævis institutio, quæ in Ecclesia traditur. Græcè παράδοσις[?].
units.tr: TRADITION (as we use the term in the Church) is any institution that is handed down in the Church. In Greek paradosis [παράδοσις].

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Eaq; PRIMO' est vel dogmatum vel rituum.
units.tr: And it is firstly either of doctrines or of rites.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Traditio dogmatum, est institutio de fide vel de bonis operibus. Hoc sensu usurpatur traditionis nomen 2. Thessal. 2.15. Nempe igitur, fratres, perstate & retinete traditiones, quas edocti estis sive per sermonem, sive per epistolam nostram. & 2. Thessal 3.6. Denunciamus autem vobis, fratres, in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ut subducatis vos ab omni fratre qui inordinatè incedit, & non secundum traditionè, quam accepit á nobis.
units.tr: A tradition of doctrines is an institution about faith or good works. In this sense the name tradition is used, 2 Thess. 2:15. So then, brethren, stand firm and hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or by our letter. And 2 Thess. 3:6. Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition which he received from us.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Traditio rituum, est institutio de observandis certis in Ecclesia ritibus.
units.tr: The tradition of rites is an institution concerning the observance of certain rites in the Church.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Estq; vel perpetua, vel temporaria.
units.tr: It is either perpetual or temporary.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Perpetua, est quæ semper necessario in universis Ecclesiis immutabiliter observari debet.
units.tr: A perpetual tradition is that which must always be observed necessarily and unchangeably in all churches.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Qualis est traditio Baptismi & Cœnæ Domini. De illo ait Basilius lib. 3 contra Eunom. Hoc palàm oppugnat sacri Baptismatis traditionem, Euntes baptizate in nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti. De hac verò Paulus 1. Cor. 11.23. Ego enim accepi à Domino, quod & tradidi vobis, Dominum Iesum videlicet, eâ nocte qua proditus est, accepisse panem, &c.
units.tr: Such is the tradition of Baptism and of the Lord's Supper. Concerning the former Basil says, in book 3 against Eunomius: This plainly opposes the tradition of holy Baptism: Go and baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. But concerning the latter, Paul, 1 Cor. 11:23: For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, namely that the Lord Jesus, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread, etc.

units.la: IIX.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Traditio temporaria, est quæ pro circumstantiarum ratione mutari potest, ac propterea libera ejus est observatio ac nequaquam absolute necessaria.
units.tr: A temporary tradition is that which can be changed according to circumstances, and therefore its observance is free and by no means absolutely necessary.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Qualis fuit Apostolica traditio de abstinentia à sanguine & suffocato. Act. 15. 28. 29. & 16.4. Paulus & Timotheus tradebant Ecclesijs servanda instituta illa quæ decreta fuerat ab Apostolis & Presbyteris q; Hierosolymis erat.
units.tr: Such was the apostolic tradition concerning abstinence from blood and from what is strangled, Acts 15:28, 29 and 16:4. Paul and Timothy handed on to the churches the institutions to be observed, which had been decreed by the apostles and the elders who were at Jerusalem.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Quales fuerunt traditiones, quæ ad εὐταξίαν[?] & externam politiam in Ecclesiasticis conventibus servandam pertinuerunt: de quib. loquitur Paulus 1. Cor. 11. 2. Laudo verò vos, fratres, quòd omnia mea meministis, & sicut tradidi vobis, traditiones retinetis.
units.tr: Such were the traditions which pertained to keeping good order and external polity in ecclesiastical assemblies, of which Paul speaks, 1 Cor. 11:2. I commend you, brethren, that you remember me in all things and hold fast the traditions just as I delivered them to you.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: SECUNDO' traditio vel divina est vel humana.
units.tr: Secondly, tradition is either divine or human.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Traditio divina, est quæ á Deo Ecclesia est commendata per Prophetas & Apostolos.
units.tr: A divine tradition is that which has been committed by God to the Church through the Prophets and Apostles.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Eaq; vel scripta est vel non scripta.
units.tr: And it is either written or unwritten.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Traditio divina scripta, est ipsa Sacra Scriptura Prophetica & Apostolica. Sic scribit Paulus 1. Cor. 15. 3. 4. Traditi enim vobis in primis, quod & accepi, Christum videlicet mortuum esse pro peccatis nostris, secundum Scripturas: & sepultum fuisse & suscitatum tertio die, secundum Scripturas.
units.tr: Divine written tradition is Holy Scripture itself, prophetic and apostolic. So Paul writes in 1 Cor. 15. 3, 4: For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received: how that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the Scriptures.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Traditio divina non scripta, est quae viva voce tradita, sed in sacrum Canonem deinceps non relata fuit.
units.tr: Unwritten divine tradition is that which was handed down by the living voice, but was afterwards not included in the sacred Canon.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Quales Apostolicae traditiones fuerunt de ordine in Ecclesia Corinthiaca servando, ab Apostolo Paulo datae: de quibus ait 1. Cor. 10. 34. Reliqua vero, cum venero, ordinabo.
units.tr: What were the apostolic traditions, delivered by the Apostle Paul, concerning the order to be kept in the Corinthian Church? Of these he says, 1 Cor. 11. 34: "The rest I will set in order when I come."

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Hujusmodi traditiones pro temporum, locorum & personarum ratione commutabiles fuerunt.
units.tr: Traditions of this kind were changeable according to the circumstances of times, places and persons.

units.la: XIIX.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Nec fuerunt his quae scriptae sunt contrariae: nec enim Deus secum ipse pugnat, & aliud viva voce, aliud scriptis tradit.
units.tr: Nor were these contrary to what has been written: for God does not contradict himself, nor does he deliver one thing by the living voice and another in writings.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Nec fuerunt immodicae.
units.tr: Nor were they excessive.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Nec inutiles: sed ad aedificationem Ecclesiae pertinentes.
units.tr: Not useless, but pertaining to the edification of the Church.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Nec conjunctae cum opinione necessitatis ad salutem.
units.tr: Nor joined with the opinion of necessity for salvation.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: De illis in genere scitur, quod ad & τάξιαν politiae Ecclesiasticae pertinuerint.
units.tr: It is known in general about those things that they pertained to the order [τάξιν] of the ecclesiastical polity.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Quales autem in specie fuerint, ignoratur.
units.tr: What kind of traditions they were in particular, however, is not known.

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Ideo Apostolicae traditiones non scriptae, de quibus certo cognitum sit, quod ab Apostolis sint traditae, nunc nullae sunt.
units.tr: Therefore the apostolic unwritten traditions, of which it is known with certainty that they were handed down by the Apostles, do not now exist.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Contrà,Bellarminus lib.4. De verbo Dei cap.5: contendit esse aliquas veras traditiones: intellige non scriptas.
units.tr: On the contrary, Bellarmine (De verbo Dei, book 4, chapter 5) contends that there are some true traditions, namely unwritten ones.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Ad id probandum utitur duobus primarys argumentis: (reliqua enim nō sunt ex fundamentalibus principijs deprom ta) sed legibus Syllogisticis ubiq; neglectis: ad quas nos omnia ejus, ut τρόπῳ [?] παιδείας [?] requirit, revocabimus.
units.tr: To prove this he uses two primary arguments (for the rest are not drawn from fundamental principles), but he ignores the rules of syllogism throughout. To those rules we shall reduce all his arguments, as the manner of instruction [τρόπῳ παιδείας] requires.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Primum Argumentum hoc est: Si Scriptura non continet omnia; sequitur esse traditiones non scriptas. At prius est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: The first argument is this: If Scripture does not contain everything, it follows that there are unwritten traditions. But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Connexi consequentiam probat: quia alioquin Deus non bene providisset Ecclesiæ. Assumtionem probat precedente capite 4. duodecim prosyllogismis habentibus inductionem dogmatum, quæ in Scriptura non continentur. Primus prossyllogismus est: Si in Scriptura nusquam extat, quo remedio fœminæ à peccato originali fuerint purgatæ; tum Scriptura non continet omnia. At prius est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: He proves the consequence of this connection, because otherwise God would not have provided well for the Church. He proves the assumption in the preceding chapter 4, with twelve prosyllogisms that bring in doctrines which are not contained in Scripture. The first prosyllogism is: If nowhere in Scripture is it found by what remedy women were cleansed from original sin, then Scripture does not contain everything. But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: RESP. Falsa est assumtio: quia Scriptura docet, quòd omnes credentes sanguis Iesu Christi purget ab omni peccato: ergo etiam fœminas veteris testamenti ab originali peccato: sicut dicitur 1.Ioh.2 2. Et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris: nec pro nostris solùm, sed etiā pro totius mundi peccatis. Et Iesa.53.5. & sequentibus: Ipse dolore assicitur ob defectiones nostras, atteritur ob iniquitates nostras: castigatio pacis nostræ imponitur ei, & tumicē ejus fit curatio nobis, &c. Ephes.2 16. Et utrosq; in uno corpore reconciliaret Deo per crucem. Rom.5.19. Sicut per inobedientiam unius hominis, peccatores constituti sunt multi: ita per unius obedientiam, justi constituentur multi. Hebr.9 26. Christus nunc semel in consummatione seculorum, ad peccatum per immolationem suiipsius abolendū patefactus. & 10.14. Unica oblatione cõsecravit in perpetuum eos qui sanctificantur. Hebr.13.8. Iesus Christus heri & hodie idem est, & in secula. Apoc.13.8. Agnus mactatus est á jactis mundi fundamentis. Ex his constat, omnes credentes tam in ve teri, quàm in novo testamento sanguine Christi mundatos esse á peccatis : Ergo etiam credentes mulieres, de quibus non minùs intelligenda sunt dicta allegata, quàm de viris.
units.tr: Answer: The assumption is false, because Scripture teaches that the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses all believers from all sin; therefore also the women of the Old Testament from original sin, as it is said in 1 John 2:2: "And he is the propitiation for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world." And Isaiah 53:5 and following: "He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was laid upon him, and with his stripes we are healed," etc. Ephesians 2:16: "and that he might reconcile both to God in one body by the cross." Romans 5:19: "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one many shall be made righteous." Hebrews 9:26: "now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself." And 10:14: "For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified." Hebrews 13:8: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever." Revelation 13:8: "the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world." From these things it is established that all believers, both in the Old Testament and in the New, have been cleansed from sins by the blood of Christ. Therefore also believing women, of whom the passages cited are to be understood no less than of men.

units.la: Instat Bellarminus: At pro masculis instituta erat Circu cisio, quâ tanquam remedio á peccato originali purgarentur : quid autem esset pro foeminis, nusquâ habet Scriptura. Resp. Instantia prius membrum est ambiguum, posterius vero falsum. Primò enim circumcisio non erat proprié re-medium quo purgarentur viri á peccato originali; purgati enim sunt proprie sanguine & spiritu Christi ab omni peccato, ac proinde etiam á peccato originali : sed erat proprié, circumcisio illius remedy Sacramentum, quo significabatur & obsignabatur credentibus, tam verè corda ipsorum circumcidi & ab illis peccata auferri, quàm verè præputij pellicula á corpore auferretur. At si Iesuita ita sentit de circumcisione, quasi illa proprie & quidem ex opere operato remedium fuisset adversus peccatum originale, errat. Secundò salsum est, nusquam haberi in Scriptura quale sacramentum esset pro foeminis institutum. Nam primò baptizatæ sunt ipsæ quoq; nube & mari: ederunt & ipsæ manna: biberunt & ipsæ aquam è petra profluentem : circumcisionis vis ad ipsas quoq; pertinuit, vi fœderis cum patribus ipsarum initi : ita ut non tantùm ipsi circumcisi mares, sed etiam semen eorum ad fedus gratiæ pertineret, juxta formulam fœderis: Ero Deus tuus & feminis tui: ergo etiam fœmellarum. Hinc non modò viri Israëlitæ, sed etiam fœminæ incircumcisis opponūtur; ut Gen.34.14. Non possumus facere rem istam, dare sororem nostram viro,cui est præputium. Hinc etiam filiæ Abrahami appellantur, Luc. 13.16. Hanc autem filiam Abrahami, quam vinxerat Satanas ecce decem & octo annos, non oportuit á vinculo isto solvi die Sabbathi? Præterea Sacramenta ipsis erant, sacrificia & oblationes, quibus ad Christum ducebantur.
units.tr: Bellarmine presses the point: But circumcision was instituted for males, by which as a remedy they were cleansed from original sin; but what was the remedy for females, Scripture nowhere says. Answer: The first part of the objection is ambiguous, the latter false. For first, circumcision was not properly the remedy by which men were cleansed from original sin; for they were properly cleansed by the blood and Spirit of Christ from all sin, and therefore also from original sin. But circumcision was properly the sacrament of that remedy, by which it was signified and sealed to believers that their hearts were truly circumcised and their sins taken away from them, just as truly as the foreskin's skin is removed from the body. But if the Jesuit thinks of circumcision as though it were properly, and indeed by the work done (ex opere operato), a remedy against original sin, he is in error. Second, it is false that Scripture nowhere shows what sacrament was instituted for women. For first, they too were baptized in the cloud and in the sea; they too ate the manna; they too drank the water flowing from the rock. The force of circumcision pertained to them as well, by virtue of the covenant made with their fathers, so that not only the circumcised males but also their seed belonged to the covenant of grace, according to the formula of the covenant: "I will be God to you and to your seed"; therefore also to the female children. Hence not only Israelite men but also women are set over against the uncircumcised, as in Genesis 34:14: "We cannot do this thing, to give our sister to one that is uncircumcised." Hence also they are called daughters of Abraham, Luke 13:16: "And ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan hath bound, lo, these eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the sabbath day?" Moreover, the sacraments for them were sacrifices and oblations, by which they were led to Christ.

units.la: Prosyllogismus II.
units.tr: Second prosyllogism.

units.la: Si in Scriptura nusquam extat, quod fuerit remedium pro masculis morientibus ante octavum diem, quo solo poterant circumcidi; tum non continet omnia. Sed prius est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If nowhere in Scripture is it found what was the remedy for males who died before the eighth day, the only day on which they could be circumcised, then Scripture does not contain everything. But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: RESPON: Assumtio primò est falsa. Nam ut adulti & circumcisi: ita etiam infantes electi ad vitam æternam, ante diem octavum morientes, sanguine & spiritu Christi exhibendi, à peccatis fuerunt mundati: sicut dicitur Iesa. 53.5. tumice ejus fit curatio nobis. & v.10. exponebat seipsē sacrificium pro reatu. Quæ[?] dicta non tantum de adultorum, sed etiam infantum curatione sunt accipienda. Deinde est ambigua: nam per remedium intelligi potest vel meritum Christi vel Sacramentum: sed Iesuita potius Sacramentum intelligit, ut colligi potest ex verbis illis, quo solo poterant circumcidi. Si de merito Christi exhibendi intelligas falsa est: sin de Sacramentis, vera quidem erit assumtio, nullum videlicet Sacramentum commemorari, quo infantes ante octavum diem essent usi: sed ineptum est, negato solo instrumento, negare rem quæ citra instrumentum effici potest. Qualis enim est ista ratiocinatio: Sacramento caruerunt: ergo remedio quo à peccatis mundarentur caruerunt? Salus quippe non pendet à Sacramentis, sed à solo Christo, sanguine & spiritu suo nos ab omni peccato purgante.
units.tr: Answer: The assumption is first of all false. For just as adults and the circumcised, so also infants chosen to eternal life who died before the eighth day were cleansed from sins by the blood and Spirit of Christ, who is to be presented to them. As it is said in Isaiah 53:5, "with his stripes we are healed," and verse 10, "he gave himself as a sacrifice for guilt." These sayings are to be understood not only of the healing of adults but also of infants. Furthermore, the assumption is ambiguous, for by "remedy" one may understand either the merit of Christ or the sacrament. But the Jesuit rather means the sacrament, as can be gathered from those words "by which alone they could be circumcised." If you understand it of the merit of Christ to be presented, it is false; but if of the sacraments, the assumption will indeed be true, namely that no sacrament is mentioned which infants before the eighth day used. But it is foolish, when the instrument alone is denied, to deny the thing which can be effected without the instrument. For what kind of reasoning is this: They lacked a sacrament, therefore they lacked the remedy by which they were cleansed from sins? Salvation indeed does not depend on the sacraments, but on Christ alone, who cleanses us from all sin by his blood and Spirit.

units.la: Prosyllogismus III.
units.tr: Prosyllogism III.

units.la: Si de gentilium in Veteri testamento justificatione à peccatis nihil in Scriptura habetur: tum illa non omnia continet. Sed illud est: Ergo & hoc.
units.tr: If nothing is found in Scripture about the justification from sins of the Gentiles in the Old Testament, then Scripture does not contain everything. But the first is true. Therefore the second is too.

units.la: RESPON: Assumtio est falsa. Nam fide in Messiam futurum tám proselytos quám Iudæos justificatos fuisse Scriptura docet. Sic .n. de Rahab dicitur Hebr. 11.31. Per fidem Rahab meretrix illa non perÿt unâ cum ÿs qui non obedierant, cum pacificé excepisset hospitio exploratores. In genere veró de omnibus dicitur Hebr.11.6. Fieri non potest ut sine fide quisquam ei placeat. Hinc promtum est colligere, proselytos quoq;, quicunq; Deo accepti fuerunt, fide placuisse. Deinde quod ad externa media, hoc est Pascha, sacrificia & oblationes attinet, eadem lex erat Iudaeis & proselytis. Num. 9. 14. & 15. 15. 29. 30. & 35.15. unde sequitur etiam ad ea, quae per sacrificia significabantur, eandem utrisq; legem fuisse.
units.tr: ANSWER: The assumption is false. For Scripture teaches that proselytes as well as Jews were justified through faith in the Messiah who was to come. So Hebrews 11:31 says of Rahab: "By faith the harlot Rahab did not perish with those who did not obey, after she had received the spies peaceably into her house." Generally, Hebrews 11:6 says of all: "It is impossible to please God without faith." From this it is easy to conclude that proselytes too, whoever were accepted by God, pleased him by faith. Further, as regards the external means, that is the Passover, the sacrifices and the offerings, the same law applied to Jews and proselytes: Numbers 9:14; 15:15, 29, 30; 35:15. Hence it follows that the same law also governed those things which were signified by the sacrifices.

units.la: Prosyllogismus IV.
units.tr: Prosyllogism IV.

units.la: Si ex Scriptura nullo modo haberi potest, extare libros aliquos veré divinos; tum non omnia continet. At prius est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If it can in no way be had from Scripture that there are some books truly divine, then Scripture does not contain everything. But the first is true. Therefore the second is too.

units.la: RESPON. Assumtio est falsa. Nam diserté dicitur 2. Tim. 3.16. Tota Scriptura divinitus est inspirata. Et 2. Pet.1.21. Non enim libitu hominis allata est olim prophetia, sed acti á Spiritu Sancto loquuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Ita Apostoli testantur libros Propheticos esse veré divinos. Et de Epistolis Pauli testatur Petrus 2.Pet.3.15. Domini nostri patientiam, salutem ducite, sicut & charus frater noster Paul. pro sibi DATA sapientia scripsit vobis.
units.tr: ANSWER. The assumption is false. For 2 Timothy 3:16 plainly says: "All Scripture is given by inspiration of God." And 2 Peter 1:21: "For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man, but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Spirit." So the Apostles testify that the prophetic books are truly divine. And Peter bears witness concerning the Epistles of Paul, 2 Peter 3:15: "Account the patience of our Lord as salvation, as also our beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, has written to you."

units.la: Exceptio. Etiamsi Scriptura dicat, libros Prophetarum & Apostolorum esse divinos: tamen non certó id credam, nisi prius credidero, Scripturam, quae hoc dicit, esse divinam. Nam etiam in Alcorano Mahumeti passim legimus, ipsum Alcoranum de coelo á Deo missum, & tamen ei nō credimus.
units.tr: Objection. Even if Scripture says that the books of the Prophets and Apostles are divine, yet I would not believe this with certainty unless I had first believed that the Scripture which says this is divine. For we also read everywhere in the Qur'an of Muhammad that the Qur'an itself was sent from heaven by God, and yet we do not believe it.

units.la: RESPON. Impia est haec exceptio dupliciter. Primo quia Petro testanti Propheticos & Apostolicos libros esse divinos fidem improbé derogat. Ac mirandum profectó, Iesuitam qui autoritatem sedis Apostolicae defendendā suscepit, Petri Apostoli autoritatem enervare, á qua reliquorum Pontificum Romanorum autoritatem pendere gloriantur. Et quae haec est improbitas, Papae Romano hodie aliquid pro divino proserenti, certó credere: Petro Apostolo autem nō certó credere? Deinde impium est,Scriptura & nominatim Petri & Pauli Apostolorum assever ationem comparare assever ationi Alcorani: & utramq; æqualem facere: nec magis Petro & Paulo credere, quàm ‿Alcorano.
units.tr: ANSWER. This objection is impious in two ways. First, because it wrongly disparages the faith due to Peter, who testifies that the prophetic and apostolic books are divine. And it is truly astonishing that a Jesuit, who has undertaken to defend the authority of the Apostolic See, should weaken the authority of the Apostle Peter, on whom the Roman Pontiffs boast that their own authority depends. And what sort of consistency is it to believe with certainty the Roman Pope today when he puts forward something as divine, but not to believe with certainty the Apostle Peter? Second, it is impious to set the assertion of Scripture, especially of the Apostles Peter and Paul, beside the assertion of the Qur'an, and to make the two equal, so that we believe Peter and Paul no more than the Qur'an.

units.la: Instantia. Cùm fides nitatur verbo Dei,nisi habeamus verbum Dei non scriptum,nulla nobis erit fides. RESP. Falsum est hoc connexum, quia repugnat Scripturæ assever anti fidem ex scriptura hauriri. Act. 17. 11. 12 Beroenses receperunt sermone cum omni alacritate, quotidie scrutantes Scripturas an hæc ita se haberent: Multi igitur crediderunt ex eis. Hinc Christus jubet scrutari Scripturas,ex quibus quid sit credendum discimus, Ioh. 5. 39. Scrutamini Scripturas,quia vos videmini vobis in ipsis vitam æternam habere: & illæ sunt quæ testantur de me. Imo qui Scripturæ non credunt,nullam fidem habent: sicut ait Christus Ioh. 5. 46. 47. Si crederetis Mosi, crederetis mihi: nam ille de me scripsit. Quód si scriptis illius nō creditis, quomodo verbis meis credetis? Et Abrahamus Luc. 16. 31. Si Mosen & Prophetas nō audiunt, nefi[?] quidem quispiam ex mortuis resurgat, fidem ei habebūt. Ex his liquere potest,an ullam fidem habeat Iesuitæ,qui Scriptura aliquid affirmanti non credunt. Notanda enim sunt verba Bellarmini supra allegata: ETIAM SI SCRIPTURA DICAT, libros Prophetarum & Apostolorum esse divinos: TAMEN NON CERTO ID CREDAM, nisi prius credidero, Scripturam quæ hoc dicit, esse divinam. Adeóne parum fidei meretur Paulus & Petrus apud Iesuitas, asseverantes scripta Prophetica & Apostolica esse divina, nisi ex traditionibus non scriptis persuadeantur boni illi scilicet Catholici, Scripturam Pauli & Petri esse divinam? Quis non videt, Iesuitas plus auctoritatis traditionibus non scriptis attribuere, quàm scriptis Pauli & Petri Apostolorum? ut quibus credere nō possint, nisi habeant verbum non scriptum quo persuadeantur ut Apostolis credat? O egregie fideles Catholicos!
units.tr: Instance. Since faith rests on the Word of God, unless we have an unwritten Word of God, we shall have no faith. ANSWER. This consequence is false, because it contradicts Scripture, which asserts that faith is drawn from Scripture. Acts 17:11–12: "The Bereans received the word with all readiness, searching the Scriptures daily whether these things were so. Therefore many of them believed." Hence Christ bids us search the Scriptures, from which we learn what is to be believed, John 5:39: "Search the Scriptures, for you think that in them you have eternal life, and it is they which testify of me." Indeed those who do not believe Scripture have no faith at all, as Christ says John 5:46–47: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote of me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?" And Abraham Luke 16:31: "If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be persuaded though one rose from the dead." From these things it can be clear whether the Jesuits have any faith at all, who do not believe anyone who affirms something from Scripture. For the words of Bellarmine quoted above must be noted: EVEN IF SCRIPTURE SAYS that the books of the Prophets and Apostles are divine: YET I WOULD NOT BELIEVE THIS WITH CERTAINTY unless I had first believed that the Scripture which says this is divine. Does Paul and Peter then deserve so little faith among the Jesuits, when they assert that the prophetic and apostolic writings are divine, unless those good Catholics are persuaded by unwritten traditions that the writings of Paul and Peter are divine? Who does not see that the Jesuits attribute more authority to unwritten traditions than to the writings of the Apostles Paul and Peter, since they cannot believe them unless they have an unwritten word by which they are persuaded to believe the Apostles? O excellent faithful Catholics!

units.la: Si nullo modo potest haberi ex Scriptura, quae sit illa Scriptura divina, tum non omnia continet. Sed illud est: Ergo & hoc.
units.tr: If it can in no way be had from Scripture which Scripture is divine, then Scripture does not contain everything. But the first is true. Therefore the second is too.

units.la: Respon. Assumtio est falsa. Nam Scripturam Propheticam ex qua passim testimonia citantur in novo Testamento, ait Paulus esse divinitus inspiratam. Illa autem est Scriptura veteris Testamenti. Et Scriptura novi Testamenti esse divinam inde patet, quia aeque est fundamentum Ecclesiae, atqs Scriptura Prophetica, Eph. 2. 20. Superstructi super fundamentum Apostolorum ac Prophetarum. Ecclesiam vero non nisi super divinum fundamentum superstrui necesse est.
units.tr: Answer. The assumption is false. For Paul says that the prophetic Scripture, from which testimonies are cited throughout the New Testament, was divinely inspired. That is the Scripture of the Old Testament. And that the Scripture of the New Testament is divine is clear from this, that it is equally the foundation of the Church as the prophetic Scripture is: Ephesians 2:20, "built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets." But the Church can be built only upon a divine foundation.

units.la: Assumtionis probatio duplex. Prima, Quomodo n. colligemus ex Scriptura, Euangelia Marci & Lucae esse vera, Euangelia Thomae & Bartholomaei esse falsa? cum ratio potius dicet, magis credendum libro praferenti titulu Apostoli, quam non Apostoli.
units.tr: The proof of the assumption is twofold. First: how shall we gather from Scripture that the Gospels of Mark and Luke are true, and that the Gospels of Thomas and Bartholomew are false? For reason would rather say that one should believe more the book which carries the title of an Apostle than one which does not.

units.la: Respon. Falsum est, ex Scriptura colligi non posse, Euangelia Marci & Lucae esse vera. Nam ipsa Euangelia Marci & Lucae suo testimonio se comprobant: omnia in illis coelestem doctrinam redolent: manifeste in illis divina sapientia dispensatio elucet: in admirationem rapiunt, rerum magis dignitate, quam verborum lenocinijs: vivide afficiunt legentium animos: admiranda harmonia cum aliorum Euangelistarum libris & scriptis aliis Propheticis & Apostolis congruunt: & ut alia omittam, ostendunt vere & perfecte modum adipiscendi aeterna salutem, & ab Ecclesia semper fuerunt recepta. At Euangelia quae sub Bartholomaei & Thomae nominibus falso circumferuntur, vera non sunt: quia in eis plurima sunt, quae Apostolicae fidei regula & sana doctrina condemnat, ut loquitur de iis Augustinus lib. 1. de consensu Euangelist. cap 1. Mutuatus est autem hoc argumetum Bellarminus ab Eccio, qui tamen assertata scribit: Nam ait Marcus & Luca nūquam vidisse Christum: & nihilominus fatetur illos é numero septuaginta discipulorum fuisse, quos Christus hinc inde prædicatum in Oppida Judæa ablegarat.
units.tr: Answer. It is false that it cannot be gathered from Scripture that the Gospels of Mark and Luke are true. For the Gospels of Mark and Luke confirm themselves by their own testimony: everything in them breathes heavenly teaching, the wisdom of God shines plainly in them, they carry the reader away with admiration, more by the dignity of the things than by the charm of words, they vividly move the minds of readers, and they agree with a wonderful harmony with the books of the other Evangelists and with the other prophetic and apostolic writings. And, to omit other points, they show truly and perfectly the way of attaining eternal salvation, and they have always been received by the Church. But the Gospels which are falsely circulated under the names of Bartholomew and Thomas are not true, because they contain many things which the rule of apostolic faith and sound doctrine condemn, as Augustine says of them in book 1 of On the Harmony of the Evangelists, chapter 1. Bellarmine borrowed this argument from Eck, who nevertheless wrote it rashly. For he says that Mark and Luke never saw Christ, and yet he admits that they were among the seventy disciples whom Christ sent out two by two into the towns of Judea.

units.la: Probatio secunda.
units.tr: Second proof.

units.la: Et unde colligam, epistolam ad Romanos esse veré Pauli, epistolam ad Laodicenses, quæ nunc circumfertur, non esse Pauli? cúm utraq; præferat titulum Pauli: & cúm Paulus in epistola ad Colossenses, cap.ult.dicat, se scripsisse ad Laodicenses, nusquam autem dicat, se scripsisse ad Romanos?
units.tr: And how shall I infer that the epistle to the Romans is truly Paul's, but the epistle to the Laodiceans, which is now circulated, is not Paul's, since both bear the title of Paul; and since Paul says in Colossians, last chapter, that he wrote to the Laodiceans, yet nowhere says that he wrote to the Romans?

units.la: RESPON. Epistolā ad Romanos, esse veré Pauli, colligitur ex ipsa epistola ad Romanos, in qua prima ejus pars, Exordiū videlicet, autorem epistolæ diserté ostendit: Paulus servus Iesu Christi, ex Dei vocatione Apostolus, separatus ad prædicandū Evangeliū Dei, &c. Quód autē Jesuita asseverat, Apostolū nusquā dicere, se scripsisse ad Romanos, in eo tū impudentiā, tum supinam negligētiam suam declarat. Nā an non dicit, se scripsisse epistolā, qui se ejus autore ὑπογραφὴ sua profitetur, ut Paulus mox initio epistolæ ad Romanos facit? An non dicit Rom.15.15. Audacule scripsi vobis, fratres, aliquatenus, &c.
units.tr: RESPONSE. That the epistle to the Romans is truly Paul's is gathered from the epistle itself, whose opening part clearly shows its author: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, separated to preach the Gospel of God," etc. As for the Jesuit's assertion that the Apostle nowhere says he wrote to the Romans, in this he displays both his impudence and his supine negligence. For does not he say that he wrote a letter who professes himself its author by subscription [ὑπογραφή], as Paul does at once at the beginning of the epistle to the Romans? Does he not say at Rom. 15.15: "I have written to you, brethren, rather boldly in some measure," etc.?

units.la: Epistola deinceps ad Laodicenses quæ veré Pauli sit, nulla extat. Nam quæ nunc circumfertur, Apostolico nomine plané est indigna, sicut ait Hierony. in catalogo in Paulo: Legunt quidam ad Laodicenses, sed ab omnibus exploditur. Et Patres Nicenæ Synodi secundæ Act.6. Inter epistolas (inquiunt) Apostoli quædam fertur ad 'Laodicéses, quam Patres nostri, tanquam alienam reprobaverunt.
units.tr: Next, there is no extant epistle to the Laodiceans that is truly Paul's. For the one now circulated is plainly unworthy of the apostolic name, as Jerome says in his catalogue, under Paul: "Some read it, as to the Laodiceans, but it is rejected by all." And the Fathers of the Second Nicene Synod, Act. 6: "Among the epistles of the Apostle (they say) one is carried about to the Laodiceans, which our Fathers rejected as alien."

units.la: Quód vero ait Jesuita, Paulum in epistola ad Colossenses cap. ult.v. 16.dicere, se scripsisse ad Laodicenses, falsum est. Non enim ait ibi, se ad Laodicenses scripsisse, sed jubet saltem Colossenses legere epistolam scriptam Laodicea. Epistola igitur illa non est scripta ad Laodicenses: quia est scripta ἐκ Λαοδικείας. Nec Pauli est illa ἐκ Λαοδικηνῶν[?] epistola: sed Laodicensium ad Paulum, ut Chrysostomus & Oecumenius aperte scribunt.
units.tr: But the Jesuit's claim that Paul says in Colossians, last chapter, verse 16, that he wrote to the Laodiceans is false. For he does not say there that he wrote to the Laodiceans; he only bids the Colossians read the epistle written from Laodicea. That epistle, therefore, was not written to the Laodiceans, because it was written from Laodicea [ἐκ Λαοδικείας]. Nor is it Paul's epistle "from the Laodiceans" [ἐκ Λαοδικηνῶν?], but the Laodiceans' epistle to Paul, as Chrysostom and Oecumenius clearly write.

units.la: Si ex Scriptura haberi non potest in particulari, libros Canonicos qui sunt in manibus, esse veré illos, qui á Prophetis & Apostol. scripti sunt, exēpli gratia, Euägelium Marci, quod nūc legimus, esse illud verū & incorruptū, q scripsit Marcus; tum Scriptura nō omnia cōtinet. At primū: Ergo & postremū.
units.tr: If it cannot be had from Scripture in particular that the canonical books in our hands are truly those written by the Prophets and Apostles (for example, that the Gospel of Mark which we now read is the true and uncorrupted one that Mark wrote), then Scripture does not contain everything. But the first: therefore also the last.

units.la: RESPON. Assumtio est falsa. Nam ex Scriptura in particulari habetur, libros illos qui nūc sunt in manibus, veré esse illorum quibus adscribuntur: ut Euägelium [?]Marci quod nunc legimus, veré est [?]Marci: quia id testatur titulus libri. Quod si cui hoc nō satisfacit, pari ratione omnes omnium antiquorum, Ecclesiasticorum, Philosophorum & Historicorum libros in dubium vocet: an veré sint illorum, quibus sunt adscripti: atq; ita Pyrrhonicam de omnibus dubitationē introducat. Sed quæ hæc est perversitas, credere libros Platoni adscriptos, veré esse illos quos scripsit Plato, quia Platonis nomen præ se ferunt: [?]Marci vero Euangelium nō credere esse verum illud Marci Euangelium, licet nomen Marci tot jam ordine labentibus seculis ab Apostolorum usq; tempore habuerit præfixum, nullis veré fidelibus contrá disputantibus, præter istos improbos Iesuitas cum impuris Manichæis, Cerdonianis, Marcionitis & Ebionæis?
units.tr: RESPONSE. The assumption is false. For it is had from Scripture in particular that the books now in our hands are truly by those to whom they are ascribed: thus the Gospel of Mark which we now read is truly Mark's, because the title of the book testifies to it. But if this does not satisfy someone, then by the same reasoning let him call into doubt all the books of all the ancient churchmen, philosophers and historians, whether they are truly by those to whom they are ascribed, and so introduce Pyrrhonian doubt about everything. But what perversity is this: to believe that the books ascribed to Plato are truly those Plato wrote, because they bear Plato's name, yet not to believe that the Gospel of Mark is the true Gospel of Mark, although it has had Mark's name prefixed to it through the many centuries that have slipped by since the time of the Apostles, with no genuine believers disputing it, except those wicked Jesuits along with the impure Manichaeans, Cerdonians, Marcionites and Ebionites?

units.la: Prosyllogismus VII.
units.tr: Prosyllogism VII.

units.la: Si intelleƈtus Scripturæ non potest haberi ex Scriptura: tū non omnia continet. At primum: Ergo & postremum.
units.tr: If the meaning of Scripture cannot be had from Scripture, then it does not contain everything. But the first: therefore also the last.

units.la: RESPON. Assumtio est falsa. ut enim quisq; est optimus interpres suorum verborum: ita etiam Spiritus Sanctus in Scriptura loquens est optimus interpres Scripturæ. Hinc Beræenses non extra Scripturā, sed in Scriptura scrutati sunt sensum scripturarum á Paulo allatarum, Act.17.11. qui nihil dixit extra ea quæ Prophetæ ac Moses futura prædixerunt. Act.26.22. Hinc Paulus ait 2. Tim.3.15. Sacras literas homine sapientem reddere posse ad salutem: ergo etiam sensum Scriptura suppeditat, sine quo sapientia ista ad salute cōsistere neqt.
units.tr: RESPONSE. The assumption is false. For just as each person is the best interpreter of his own words, so the Holy Spirit, speaking in Scripture, is the best interpreter of Scripture. Hence the Bereans searched the sense of the Scriptures cited by Paul not outside Scripture but within Scripture (Acts 17.11), and Paul said nothing beyond what the Prophets and Moses foretold as future (Acts 26.22). Hence Paul says at 2 Tim. 3.15 that the holy letters are able to make a man wise unto salvation. Therefore Scripture also supplies its own sense, without which that wisdom cannot stand unto salvation.

units.la: Sed probat Iesuita assumtionem hoc modo:
units.tr: But the Jesuit proves the assumption in this way:

units.la: Saepissime Scriptura ambigua & perplexa est, ut nisi ab aliquo, qui errare non possit, explicetur, non possit intelligi. Epilogismus est talis:
units.tr: Very often Scripture is ambiguous and perplexed, so that unless it is explained by someone who cannot err, it cannot be understood. The argument runs thus:

units.la: Ex Scriptura ambigua & perlexa non potest haberi ejusdem intellectus:
units.tr: From ambiguous and perplexed Scripture its same sense cannot be had:

units.la: At sacra Scriptura est ambigua & perplexa:
units.tr: But holy Scripture is ambiguous and perplexed:

units.la: Ergo ex ea non potest haberi ejusdem intellectus.
units.tr: Therefore from it its same sense cannot be had.

units.la: RESPON. Primo Propositio non est universaliter vera. Est non vera saltem de illa Scriptura, quae prorsus tota est ambigua & perplexa, ita ut nihil in ea sit certi & perspicui. Secundo assumtio laborat elencho παρὰ τὸ μὴ ὅλον ὡς ὅλον: quae elenchum ipsemet Iesuita produt, cum fatetur saepissime Scripturam esse ambiguam & perplexam non igitur tota est ambigua & perplexa. Atqui haec confessio satis est ad ipsum refutandum: Hinc enim colligitur, declarari ambigua & perplexa loca ex illis quae non sunt ambigua & perplexa.
units.tr: RESPONSE. First, the major premise is not universally true. It is not true at least of that Scripture which is wholly ambiguous and perplexed, so that nothing in it is certain and plain. Second, the minor premise suffers from the fallacy of "not whole taken as whole" [παρὰ τὸ μὴ ὅλον ὡς ὅλον], which the Jesuit himself produces when he confesses that Scripture is very often ambiguous and perplexed; therefore it is not wholly ambiguous and perplexed. And this confession is enough to refute him, for from it it is gathered that the ambiguous and perplexed passages are explained from those which are not ambiguous and perplexed.

units.la: Instat: nisi ab aliquo, qui errare non possit, explicetur, non potest intelligi. RESP. Et is qui est tu Spiritus Sanctus in Scriptura loquens: tu ipsi Prophetae & Apostoli per Spiritum Sanctum loquentes. Alii vero interpretes Ecclesiastici omnes, nullo excepto, errare possunt, quoties ab analogia fidei in suis interpretationibus recedunt. Papam vero no errare, salsissimum esse dicimus: imo ne quidem inter infimos Ecclesiasticos interpretes numeramus, cum Antichristus ille sit, Scripturae corruptor & depravator. Qualis est enim illa interpretatio, in qua sceleratissimus filius perditionis de se audet interpretari, quae de solo IESV CHRISTO sunt intelligenda? Lib. Ceremon. Pontifical I. tit. 7.
units.tr: He insists: unless it is explained by someone who cannot err, it cannot be understood. RESPONSE: And that someone is the Holy Spirit himself speaking in Scripture, and the Prophets and Apostles speaking through the Holy Spirit. But all the other ecclesiastical interpreters, none excepted, can err, as often as they depart from the analogy of faith in their interpretations. But that the Pope does not err we say is most false; indeed we do not even count him among the lowest ecclesiastical interpreters, since he is that Antichrist, the corrupter and depraver of Scripture. For what sort of interpretation is it when that most wicked son of perdition dares to interpret of himself what must be understood of Jesus Christ alone? Lib. Ceremon. Pontifical. I. tit. 7.

units.la: Papa in nocte nativitatis Domini benedicit ensem, quem postea donat alicui principi, in signum infinitae potentiae Pontifici collatae: juxta illud, Data est mihi omnis potestas in coelo & in terra. Item dominabitur a mari usque ad mare, & a flumine usque ad terminos orbis terrarum. Et in c. quoniam, de immunit. in sexto: Nos justitiam nostram & Ecclesiae sponsae nostrae nolentes negligere, &c. Itane de se interpretari audet libidinosissimus scortator, quod sit sponsus Ecclesiæ? Atqui inter omnes constat, solius Christi hunc honorem esse proprium, ut ipse sit vir Ecclesiæ, Ecclesia vero ipsius sponsa, ut Paulus testatur 2. Cor. 11. 2. Aptavi vos, quos uni viro, ut virginē purā fistā[?], nempe Christo. Sed sufficiant in præsentia hæc Papalium interpretationum exempla.
units.tr: The Pope on the night of the Lord's nativity blesses a sword, which he afterwards gives to some prince, as a sign of the infinite power conferred on the Pontiff, according to that saying: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth." Likewise: "He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth." And in c. quoniam, de immunit. in sexto: "We, not willing to neglect our justice and that of our spouse the Church," etc. Does the most lustful fornicator dare so to interpret of himself that he is the bridegroom of the Church? Yet it is agreed by all that this honour belongs to Christ alone, that he himself is the husband of the Church and the Church his bride, as Paul testifies at 2 Cor. 11.2: "I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a pure virgin," namely to Christ. But let these examples of Papal interpretations suffice for the present.

units.la: Exempla vero quæ Bellarminus adducit probandæ assutionis causa, vid. de æqualitate divinarum personarum, de processione Spiritus Sancti à Patre & Filio, &c. prorsus sunt ἀπροσδιόνυσα: Nec enim illa probant, Scriptura esse ambigua & perplexa: sed non omnia totidem literis & syllabis in Scriptura exstare, quæ credimus: cum multa saltē bona cosequetiā ex ea deducatur.
units.tr: The examples which Bellarmine adduces to prove the assumption, namely on the equality of the divine persons, on the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, and so on, are altogether irrelevant [ἀπροσδιόνυσα], for they do not prove that Scripture is ambiguous and perplexed, but that not all the things we believe are found in Scripture in so many letters and syllables, since many good consequences are at least deduced from it.

units.la: Prosyllogismus VIII.
units.tr: Prosyllogism VIII.

units.la: Si nullū in Scriptura est testimoniū, Beatā Mariā semper fuisse virginē; tū illa nō omnia cōtinet. At illud est: Ergo & hoc. RESP. Falsa est assumtio, sive tempus ante partū, sive post partū spectes. Ante partū Maria fuisse semper virginē, expresse tradit Scriptura, Isef.7.14. Matth.1.23. Ecce virgo cōcipiet & pariet Filiū: Luc.1.34. Dixit Maria ad Angelum, Quomodo erit istud, quādoquidē virū nō novi? Matth.1.18. Quū mater ejus Maria desponsa esset Iosepho, priusquā ipsi convenissent, comperta est prægnans esse è Spiritu Sancto, & 25.[?] Sed non cognovit eam, quousq; peperisset filiū illū suum primogenitū. Post partum Mariam mansisse virginem bonā consequetiā colligitur ex Scriptura. Nā primo Scriptura nusquā affirmat, eā posteā suisse cognitā á Iosepho, aut alios liberos peperisse. Deinde Dominus in cruce pendēs matrem Iohanni commendavit, & Iohannes eā recepit domū suam: Ioh.19.27. Ergo Maria nō habuit tū maritū & liberos. Tertiō idē colligit ex Matt.1.25. Basilius in concione de Nativitate Domini: Ut ne eorum, qui Christum amant, aures suscipiant, quòd Deipara aliquādo virgo esse desijt, illa testimonia sufficientia putamus, ad hoc quidem: Non cognovit eam DONEC peperisset filium suum. Quódparticula DONEC in multis quidē locis quādam tēporis determinatiōne significare videtur: revera autē indefinitū indicat. Quale est illud,Ecce ego sum vobiscum usque ad consummationem seculi. Quartò ad idem probandum pro, ferūt locum ex Ezechiele de porta clausa Proclus Cyzicenus, Ambrosius Sermon 4. & 5. & Epistolarum lib. 10. epistol. 81. Quintò Hieronymus contra Helvidium idem multis Scripturis docet. In Scriptura ergo ἀειπαρθενία[?] Mariae traditur.
units.tr: If there is no testimony in Scripture that the Blessed Mary always remained a virgin, then Scripture does not contain everything. But the first holds: therefore the second too. REPLY: The assumption is false, whether you look at the time before the birth or the time after it. Before the birth, Scripture expressly teaches that Mary was always a virgin: Isa. 7.14; Matt. 1.23, "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son"; Luke 1.34, Mary said to the angel, "How can this be, since I do not know a man?"; Matt. 1.18, "When his mother Mary was betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child of the Holy Spirit"; and Matt. 1.25, "But he did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son." After the birth, the good consequence that Mary remained a virgin is drawn from Scripture. For, first, Scripture nowhere affirms that she was afterwards known by Joseph or bore other children. Second, the Lord, hanging on the cross, commended his mother to John, and John took her into his house: John 19.27. Therefore Mary did not then have a husband and children. Third, the same is inferred from Matt. 1.25. Basil, in his sermon on the Nativity of the Lord: "So that the ears of those who love Christ may not receive the idea that the Mother of God at some time ceased to be a virgin, we think these testimonies are sufficient for this: 'he did not know her UNTIL she had borne her son.'" The particle UNTIL seems in many places to signify some determination of time, but in truth it indicates something indefinite, as in that saying, "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." Fourth, to prove the same, Proclus of Cyzicus, Ambrose in Sermon 4 and 5, and in Epistle 81 of Book 10 of his Letters, bring forward the passage from Ezekiel about the closed gate. Fifth, Jerome in his work against Helvidius teaches the same from many passages of Scripture. Therefore the perpetual virginity [ἀειπαρθενία] of Mary is taught in Scripture.

units.la: Prosyllogismus i x.
units.tr: Prosyllogism IX.

units.la: Si in Scriptura nō exstat, in novo Testamento Pascha esse celebrandum die Dominico; tum nō omnia continet. At prius est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If it is not found in Scripture that in the New Testament the Passover is to be celebrated on the Lord's day, then Scripture does not contain everything. But the first holds: therefore the second too.

units.la: RESP. Primo Connexum est falsum. Nam etsi in Scriptura non exstaret, in novo Testamento Pascha esse celebrandum die Dominico: tamen Scriptura omnia ad salutem necessaria contineret. Distinctio enim dierum non est ad salutem necessaria, juxta sequentia dicta, Rom. 14. 5. 6. Alius quidem æstimat diem præ die: alius autem pariter æstimat quemvis diem. Unusquisq; in animo suo plenè certus esto. Qui curat diem, Domino curat: & qui non curat diem, Domino non curat. Gal. 4. 9. 10. 11. At nunc quum cognoscatis Deum, imò potius cogniti sitis à Deo, quomodo convertitis vos retrorsum ad infirma & egena elementa, quibus ad superiora regressi, servire vultis? Dies observatis & menses & tempora & annos. Metuo de vobis, ne frustra fatigatus sim apud vos. Coloss. 2. 16. Nequis igitur vos damnet ob cibum vel potū, aut respectu festi aut novilunij, aut Sabbathorum. Præterea Pascha fuit typus & ceremonia: cessavit igitur rigida ejus observatio exhibito Christo. Coloss. 2. 16. 17. Hebr. 10. 1. Exceptio. Hæretici habiti sunt ab Ecclesia antiqua Quartadecimani, hoc est, qui Judæorum exemplo Pascha decimoquarto die primi mensis celebrare solebant. Ergo celebratio Paschatis die Dominico, est ad salutem necessaria.
units.tr: REPLY. First, the connection is false. For even if it were not found in Scripture that in the New Testament the Passover is to be celebrated on the Lord's day, Scripture would nevertheless contain everything necessary to salvation. The distinction of days is not necessary to salvation, according to what follows in Rom. 14.5, 6: "One man esteems one day above another; another esteems every day alike. Let each one be fully convinced in his own mind. He who observes the day, observes it to the Lord; and he who does not observe the day, does not observe it to the Lord." Gal. 4.9-11: "But now that you have come to know God, or rather are known by God, how is it that you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you desire to be enslaved all over again? You observe days and months and seasons and years. I am afraid for you, that I have labored over you in vain." Col. 2.16: "Let no one therefore judge you in respect of food or drink, or in respect of a festival or a new moon or sabbaths." Moreover, the Passover was a type and a ceremony; its rigid observance therefore ceased when Christ was revealed: Col. 2.16, 17; Heb. 10.1. Exception: the Quartodecimans were held as heretics by the ancient Church, that is, those who, following the example of the Jews, were accustomed to celebrate the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. Therefore the celebration of the Passover on the Lord's day is necessary to salvation.

units.la: RESP. Falsa est omissa propositio conexa. Causa falsitatis est,quia Quarta decimani primó non á tota Ecclesia,sed salt-tem á Romana,eiq; adhærentibus: deinde illegitimé pro hæreticis sunt habiti: quod ex sequenti historica commemoratione patebit. Veteres non eodem die celebrabant Pascha; & Orientales quidem Ecclesiæ decimoquarto die mensis primi: Occidentales verò die Dominico, decimumquartum diem proximè sequente. Euseb. lib. 5. cap. 23. 24. Socrates lib.5. cap.22. Eratq; eo tempore liberum,ut diversis diebus Pascha haberetur. Polycarpus enim servabat morem,quem Iohannes tradiderat, & Anicetus servabat ritum, quem á superioribus acceperat. Interea tamen inter se concordiam custodiebant. Euseb. lib.5.cap.24. Sed VICTOR Episcopus Romanus,cùm vix aliquantulum sedata fuisset persecutionum procella,primus fuit qui pacem Ecclesiæ instigante Satana turbavit. Ut enim Papalem ostenderet animum, decretum fecit,ut propter memoriam resurrectionis Domini,Paschadie Dominica á quartadecima die mensis Martij usq; ad vigesimamprimam ejusdem mensis celebraretur. Scripserat etiam ad Polycratem Episcopum Ephesinum,qui præsidebat inter Episcopos Asiaticos, & pro autoritate mandaverat,ut Episcopi Asiatici consuetudinem Romanæ Ecclesiæ in celebrando Paschate sequerentur. Qua arrogantia Victoris omnes Episcopi Asiatici vehementer offensi decreto ipsius contradixerunt. Hinc sex concilia provincialia celebrata esse propter diem Paschæ, refert Eusebius lib.5. cap. 23. & 24. Multi Orientis ac Aegypti præsules decreto Victoris assensum præbebant. Odiosé diu decertatum est. Victor Asiaticos Episcopos ab Ecclesiæ communione excludere decrevit, tanquam reos hæresews, quód de Paschate Romanæ Ecclesiæ consentire nollent: quo nomine graviter fuit reprehensus etiam á suæ factionis Episcopis, nominatim verò ab Irenæo Lugdunensi Episcopo, qui per literas eum monuit, ut ageret potiús quæ pacis essent: indignum esse dicens, propter rituum & ceremoniarum dissonantiam, Ecclesiæ concordiam rumpere: utens etiam hoc argumento, quód diversitas jejuniorum nunquam unionem Ecclesiarum dissolvisset. Euseb. lib.5. cap.24. Hoc pacto res sedata: quaelibet pars suam retinuit, quam receperat consuetudinem: donec in Concilio Niceno constitutio facta est ut Pascha die Dominico celebraretur: quam in hodiernum usq; diem observat Ecclesia. Hoc schismate quod Romanus Episcopus excitavit, turbata fuit tranquillitas Ecclesiarum & doctrina de libertate Christiana in ceremonijs adiaphoris obscurata: & Asiatici qui Pascha celebrabant decimaquarta Lunæ, fuerunt appellati Quartadecimani hæretici damnati,ut Nicephorus refert lib.4.cap.39. Sed cum injuria hærefeωs[?] crimen ipsis fuit impositum: cum non sint hæretici, qui ab aliis in ceremonia alicujus observatione variant, sed qui pertinaciter nulla habita ratione admonitionum factarū Ecclesiam distrahunt & dividunt disseminatione & propugnatione erroris ejusmodi,qui vel aperte pugnat cum sacra doctrinæ fundamento,vel ex quo sequitur partis alicujus fundamenti eversio. Roman.16.17. 1.Tim.6.3. 2.Tim.3.13.
units.tr: REPLY. The omitted connected proposition is false. The cause of the falsity is that the Quartodecimans were, first, not condemned by the whole Church, but at least not by the Roman Church and those adhering to it; second, they were wrongly held as heretics, as will be clear from the following historical account. The ancients did not all celebrate the Passover on the same day: the Eastern Churches celebrated it on the fourteenth day of the first month, but the Western Churches on the Lord's day next following the fourteenth day. Eusebius, Book 5, chapters 23 and 24; Socrates, Book 5, chapter 22. At that time it was free for the Passover to be kept on different days. For Polycarp kept the custom which John had handed down, and Anicetus kept the rite which he had received from his predecessors. Meanwhile, however, they preserved concord among themselves. Eusebius, Book 5, chapter 24. But Victor, bishop of Rome, when the storm of persecutions had scarcely been calmed a little, was the first who, at the instigation of Satan, disturbed the peace of the Church. For, to show his papal spirit, he made a decree that, on account of the memory of the Lord's resurrection, the Passover should be celebrated on the Sunday from the fourteenth day of March to the twenty-first day of the same month. He had also written to Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, who presided among the Asian bishops, and by authority had ordered that the Asian bishops should follow the custom of the Roman Church in celebrating Easter. At this arrogance of Victor all the Asian bishops were greatly offended and opposed his decree. Hence, Eusebius reports, six provincial councils were held on account of the day of Easter, Book 5, chapters 23 and 24. Many prelates of the East and of Egypt gave assent to Victor's decree. The dispute was long and bitter. Victor decided to exclude the Asian bishops from communion with the Church, as guilty of heresy, because they would not agree with the Roman Church about Easter. For this he was severely rebuked even by bishops of his own party, and especially by Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, who wrote to him by letter, urging him to pursue rather what belongs to peace, saying that it was unworthy to break the concord of the Church over a difference of rites and ceremonies, and also using this argument: that the diversity of fasts had never dissolved the union of the Churches. Eusebius, Book 5, chapter 24. In this way the matter was settled: each party kept the custom it had received; until, at the Council of Nicaea, a decision was made that the Passover should be celebrated on the Lord's day, which the Church observes to this very day. By this schism, which the Roman bishop stirred up, the tranquillity of the Churches was disturbed, and the doctrine of Christian liberty in indifferent ceremonies was obscured. And the Asians who celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day of the moon were called Quartodeciman heretics and condemned, as Nicephorus reports, Book 4, chapter 39. But the charge of heresy was imposed on them unjustly, since those are not heretics who differ from others in the observance of some ceremony, but those who, obstinately and with no regard for the admonitions given, divide and tear apart the Church by spreading and defending an error of this kind, which either openly fights against the sound foundation of doctrine or from which the overthrow of some part of the foundation follows. Rom. 16.17; 1 Tim. 6.3; 2 Tim. 3.13.

units.la: Secundo, assumtio non est simpliciter vera. Etsi enim expressis verbis in Scriptura non exstat, Pascha esse celebrandum die Dominico: tamen colligi id potest ex illis locis,in quibus dicitur, Apostolos convenisse primo die hebdomadis Ioh. 20. 1.26. Alios item fideles[?]. 1.Cor.16.2.
units.tr: Second, the assumption is not simply true. For although it is not found in Scripture in express words that the Passover is to be celebrated on the Lord's day, it can nevertheless be inferred from those passages in which it is said that the apostles met on the first day of the week: John 20.1, 26; and other faithful people likewise: 1 Cor. 16.2.

units.la: Prosyllogismus x.
units.tr: Prosyllogism 10.

units.la: Si Pædobaptismus ex Scriptura probari non potest: tum ea non omnia cōtinet. Antecedens est verū: Ergo & consequēs.
units.tr: If infant baptism cannot be proved from Scripture, then Scripture does not contain all things. The antecedent is true; therefore the consequent also.

units.la: R E S P. Assumtio est falsa: Nam infantes Christianorum esse baptizandos ex Scriptura probari potest. Illa enim testatur, infantes fidelium fœderi gratia insertos. Gen.17.7. Ero Deus tuus & feminis tui post te. Testatur eorum esse regnum cœlorum Matth. 19.14. Testatur ad ipsos pertinere promissionem. Act. 2.39. Vobis & liberis vestris est facta promissio. Testatur eos sanctos esse. 1.Cor.7.14. Liberi vestri sancti sunt. Hinc bona consequentia colligimus, fidelium infantes esse baptizandos. Similiter judicavit antiquitas, Paedobaptismum esse dogma ἐγγραφον[?]: ut Cyprianus lib. 3. Epist. 8. Augustinus contra Donatist. lib. 4. cap. 23. & 24.
units.tr: REPLY. The assumption is false. For it can be proved from Scripture that the infants of Christians are to be baptized. For Scripture testifies that the infants of believers are included in the covenant of grace: Gen. 17.7, "I will be your God and the God of your seed after you." It testifies that the kingdom of heaven belongs to them: Matt. 19.14. It testifies that the promise pertains to them: Acts 2.39, "The promise is made to you and to your children." It testifies that they are holy: 1 Cor. 7.14, "Your children are holy." From this we draw the good inference that the infants of believers are to be baptized. In the same way antiquity judged that infant baptism is a dogma written down (ἐγγραφον): as Cyprian, Epistle 8, book 3; Augustine, against the Donatists, book 4, chapters 23 and 24.

units.la: Prosyllogismus XI.
units.tr: Prosyllogism 11.

units.la: Si purgatorium est, & tamen ex Scriptura probari non potest: tum ea non omnia continet. ⌣At prius est: Lutherus enim in Assertionibus artic.37. ait: Ego tamen & credo Purgatorium esse, & consulo suadeoq; credendum: & ibidem asserit, purgatorium non posse probari ex Sacris literis. Ergo erit & posterius.
units.tr: If purgatory exists, and yet it cannot be proved from Scripture, then Scripture does not contain all things. But the first is true: for Luther, in his Assertions, article 37, says: "Yet I both believe that purgatory exists, and advise and urge that it be believed." And in the same place he asserts that purgatory cannot be proved from the Holy Writings. Therefore the second is also true.

units.la: RESP. Primo Propositio est falsa. Quid enim, si fictitiū[?] purgatorium in Scriptura non traditur, propterea illa non continet omnia ad salutem necessaria? Simile est: Si donatio illa à Constantino Magno facta est Romano Papæ, & tamen ex Scriptura probari non potest: tum ea non omnia continet. Secundo etiam assumtionis pars prior, qua asseritur Purgatorium esse, falsa est: nullibi enim Scriptura docet, esse ejusmodi aliquod purgatorium, quale Pontificij fingūt: imo Scripturae é diametro repugnat. Tertio altera assumtionis pars, quâ dicitur, purgatorium non posse probari ex Sacris literis, adversatur ipsis Iesuitis. Nam si Purgatorium non potest probari ex Sacris literis; cur igitur testimonia ex Sacris literis ad purgatorij defensionem Iesuitae adducunt? Exceptio. At Bellarminus ex Lutheri falsitem[?], non ex suo sensu loquitur.
units.tr: REPLY. First, the major premise is false. For what if fictitious purgatory is not handed down in Scripture; does it therefore follow that Scripture does not contain all things necessary to salvation? It is like this: if the donation supposedly made by Constantine the Great to the Roman Pope cannot be proved from Scripture, then Scripture does not contain all things. Second, the first part of the assumption, which asserts that purgatory exists, is also false: Scripture nowhere teaches that there is any such purgatory as the Papists imagine; indeed it is diametrically opposed to Scripture. Third, the other part of the assumption, which says that purgatory cannot be proved from the Holy Writings, is at odds with the Jesuits themselves. For if purgatory cannot be proved from the Holy Writings, why then do the Jesuits bring forward testimonies from the Holy Writings in defence of purgatory? Objection: but Bellarmine speaks from Luther's falsehood, not from his own meaning.

units.la: RESP. Cùm Lutheri testimonium alleget, vel assentitur ei vel non assentitur. Si assentitur, tum concedit, Purgatorium non posse ex Sacris literis probari, atq; ita se & alios Iesuitas mendacij arguit, qui alibi ex Sacris literis purgatorium defendere conantur. Si non assentitur, cur igitur ne verbulo quidem unico indicavit, sibi Lutheri sententiam salsam videri? ⌣Ac si ei non assentitur, purgatorio patrocinium ex Scriptura deneganti: nos quoq; non obstrictisumus assentiri, Purgatorium suadenti. Qua enim ipse auctoritate teneri non volet, eâ quoq; nos devinciri non est æquum: cûm disputandi principia utrique parti communia & ab utraque parte approbata esse oporteat.
units.tr: REPLY. When he cites Luther's testimony, he either agrees with it or does not. If he agrees, then he concedes that purgatory cannot be proved from the Holy Writings, and so he convicts himself and the other Jesuits of falsehood, who elsewhere try to defend purgatory from the Holy Writings. If he does not agree, why then did he not indicate, even by a single word, that Luther's opinion seemed false to him? And if he does not agree with Luther, who denies that purgatory can be defended from Scripture, neither are we bound to agree with him, who urges purgatory. For it is not right that we should be bound by that authority which he himself does not wish to be binding on him; since the principles of disputation ought to be common to both parties and approved by both.

units.la: Prossyllogismus duodecimus.
units.tr: Prosyllogism 12.

units.la: Si in Scriptura nusquam invenitur, nullum esse Verbum Dei, nisi scriptum; tum ea non omnia continet. Antecedens est verum: Ergo & consequens.
units.tr: If nowhere in Scripture is it found that there is any Word of God except what is written, then Scripture does not contain all things. The antecedent is true; therefore the consequent also.

units.la: RESP. Primo propositionis connexio non est necessaria. Necessaria autem esset, si praeter Scripturam Propheticam & Apostolicam, hoc tempore exstaret Verbum aliquod Dei non scriptum. Quis autem est tam præsumtuosus, qui sine ullo testimonio divino affirmet hoc vel illud quod in divinis scripturis non comprehenditur, certo esse Verbum Dei? aut si audeat affirmare, unde hoc probabit? Quibus non afferentibus Scripturam, licet afferere, ea quæ proponunt, Deum dicere, nisi Prophetis & Apostolis? Deinde assumtio est falsa. Nam si præter Scripturam est nunc aliud Verbum Dei non scriptum, quare igitur Apostolus ad Verbum non scriptum non æquè fideles ablegat atq; ad Scripturas? quare dicit, Sacras literas posse hominem sapientem reddere ad salutem, 2. Tim. 3.15? Cur dicit, Scripturæ esse utilem ad perfectè reddendum hominem Dei, ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructum? Cur ista soli Scripturæ attribuit, Verbi non scripti prorsus oblitus? Proinde concludimus his prossyllogismis probatum non esse, Scripturam Sacram non omnia dogmata necessaria ad salutem continere: ac propterea etiam traditiones non scriptæ, quæ citra omnem dubitationem sint Apostolicæ, jam nullæ ostendi possunt.
units.tr: REPLY. First, the connection of the premise is not necessary. It would be necessary if, besides the prophetic and apostolic Scripture, some unwritten Word of God existed at this time. But who is so presumptuous that, without any divine testimony, he affirms with certainty that this or that, which is not contained in the divine Scriptures, is the Word of God? Or if he dares to affirm it, from what source will he prove it? Since they bring no Scripture to support it, can they assert that the things they put forward are what God says, except the Prophets and Apostles? Next, the assumption is false. For if there is now some other unwritten Word of God besides Scripture, why then does the Apostle not send believers to the unwritten Word just as he sends them to the Scriptures? Why does he say that the Holy Writings can make a man wise unto salvation, 2 Tim. 3.15? Why does he say that Scripture is profitable for making the man of God perfect, thoroughly furnished unto every good work? Why does he attribute these things to Scripture alone, if he had completely forgotten the unwritten Word? Therefore we conclude, from these prosyllogisms, that it has not been proved that Holy Scripture does not contain all doctrines necessary to salvation; and consequently that no unwritten traditions can yet be shown to be apostolic beyond all doubt.

units.la: HACTENVS PRIMVM BELLARMINI PRO[?] traditionibus argumentum refutatum est: sequitur secundum.
units.tr: Thus far the first argument of Bellarmine for traditions has been refuted; the second follows.

units.la: XXIIX.
units.tr: XXIIX.

units.la: Secundi argumenti summa huc redit:
units.tr: The sum of the second argument comes to this:

units.la: Si Scriptura testatur, esse traditiones: tum certé sunt.
units.tr: If Scripture testifies that there are traditions, then certainly there are.

units.la: Antecedens est verum: Consequens igitur.
units.tr: The antecedent is true; therefore the consequent.

units.la: Assumtio probatur undecim Scriptura testimonijs.
units.tr: The assumption is proved by eleven testimonies of Scripture.

units.la: Primum testimonium.
units.tr: First testimony.

units.la: Ioh.16.12. ait Christus: Multa habeo vobis dicere, sed non potestis portare modò.
units.tr: John 16:12, Christ says: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now."

units.la: Ergo sunt aliquæ traditiones nonscriptæ.
units.tr: Therefore there are some unwritten traditions.

units.la: Syllogismus talis erit:
units.tr: The syllogism will be this:

units.la: Si multa Apostolis á Christo fuerunt dicenda, sed quæ tum portare noluerunt; sequitur esse traditiones: Sed illud: Ergo & hoc.
units.tr: If Christ was to say many things to the Apostles which they were then unwilling to bear, it follows that there are traditions. But the former holds; therefore the latter also.

units.la: RESP. Primò Conexum laborat manifesto sophismate περὶ τὸ ἐπόμενον. Nam ex posito antecedente non sequitur esse traditiones: sed contrarium potius, vid. non esse traditiones non scriptas: quia Christus illa multa, quæ discipuli portare non potuerunt, tum non tradidit: quia tum illa non poterant portare, propter has causas. i. quia multa illis locutus est per proverbia & parabolas Ioh.16.25.11. quia occupati erant animi ipsorum communi Iudaico errore, Christum fore mundanū regem Luc.24.21. Act.1.6. iii. quia animi ipsorum erant præpediti mæstitiâ, quæ ipsos non sinebat altius exsurgere ad intelligenda ea quæ á Christo audiebant Iohan. 16.6. iv. quia laborabant adhuc naturali & ingenitâ ignorantiâ Ioh.16.12. v. quia tenebantur adhuc tarditate ad credendum Luc. 24.25. vi. quia nondum missus erat illis Spiritus sanctus Ioh.16.12.13. Propter has causas cûm multa ferre Apostoli non possent, Dominus ea tum non tradidit. Traditiones igitur hinc probari nequeunt.
units.tr: ANSWER. First, the connection labours under a manifest sophism, [περὶ τὸ ἐπόμενον]. For from the posited antecedent it does not follow that there are traditions; the contrary follows, namely that there are no unwritten traditions, because Christ did not then hand down those many things which the disciples could not bear. They could not bear them at that time for these causes: (1) because he spoke many things to them through proverbs and parables, John 16:25, 11; (2) because their minds were occupied with the common Jewish error that Christ would be a worldly king, Luke 24:21, Acts 1:6; (3) because their minds were weighed down by sadness, which did not allow them to rise higher to understand what they heard from Christ, John 16:6; (4) because they still laboured under natural and innate ignorance, John 16:12; (5) because they were still slow to believe, Luke 24:25; (6) because the Holy Spirit had not yet been sent to them, John 16:12, 13. For these causes, since the Apostles could not bear many things, the Lord did not then hand them down. Traditions therefore cannot be proved from this.

units.la: Secundò, dissentit Iesuita ab aliis Catholicis. Nam Glossa ordinaria interlinearis dicit, multa illa quæ Christus tum reticuit, neminem habere determinare: at Iesuita determinat, dum ea traditiones Papisticas esse docet. Quin etiam Nicolaus Lyranus aliter quàm Iesuita hunc locum interpretatur: Hic, inquit, ostendit Christus efficaciam Spiritus Sancti respectu Apostolorum, quæ consistit in illustratione ipsorum de profundissimis & altissimis fidei fecretis. Et paulo post. Docebit vos omnem veritatem, scil. necessariam ad salutem: non solum pro personis vestris, sed etiam ad regimē Ecclesiæ & fidelium instructionē. Quid hæc interpretatio ad traditiones non scriptas?
units.tr: Second, the Jesuit disagrees with the other Catholics. For the ordinary interlinear gloss says that no one can determine what those many things were that Christ then kept silent about; but the Jesuit determines them, when he teaches that they are Papistical traditions. Nicholas of Lyra also interprets this place differently from the Jesuit: "Here," he says, "Christ shows the efficacy of the Holy Spirit with respect to the Apostles, which consists in the illumination of them concerning the deepest and highest secrets of the faith." And a little after: "He will teach you all truth, namely that which is necessary for salvation, not only for your own persons, but also for the governing of the Church and the instruction of the faithful." What has this interpretation to do with unwritten traditions?

units.la: Secundum testimonium.
units.tr: Second testimony.

units.la: Iohan. 21. 25. dicitur: Sunt autem & alia multa, quæ fecit Iesus; quæ si scribantur singula, nec ipsum arbitror mundum capere posse eos, qui scribendi sunt libros. Constat igitur, multa Dominum fecisse & dixisse, quæ non sunt scripta.
units.tr: It is said in John 21:25: "And there are also many other things which Jesus did; which, if they were written every one, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that should be written." It is therefore clear that the Lord did and said many things which are not written.

units.la: Syllogismus talis erit:
units.tr: The syllogism will be this:

units.la: Si multa Dominus dixit & fecit, quæ nō sunt scripta, tum sunt aliquæ traditiones non scriptæ. Antecedens est verum: Ergo & consequens.
units.tr: If the Lord said and did many things which are not written, then there are some unwritten traditions. The antecedent is true; therefore the consequent also.

units.la: RESP. Connexum non est necessarium & simpliciter verum. Esset autem necessarium & simpliciter verum, si ea quæ non sunt scripta, viva voce Apostoli ita tradidissent suis auditoribus, ut propagata ad posteros extra omnem controversiam versarentur, verè á Domino esse dicta ac facta. Iam verò talia nulla proferri queunt, quæ probabiliter saltem judicari possint, esse á Domino certò dicta vel facta.
units.tr: ANSWER. The connection is neither necessary nor simply true. It would be necessary and simply true if the things that are not written had been handed down by the Apostles by word of mouth to their hearers in such a way that, propagated to posterity, they would stand beyond all controversy as truly said and done by the Lord. But no such things can be produced which could be judged, at least probably, to have been certainly said or done by the Lord.

units.la: Instantia. Constat nihilominus, multa Dominum fecisse vel dixisse, quæ non sunt scripta. Nam iflos[?] libros, qui exstat, una manus capere potest: Iohannes autem dicit, totum mundum non posse capere libros, qui scribendi essent.
units.tr: Objection. Nevertheless, it is clear that the Lord did or said many things which are not written. For one hand can hold the books that exist; but John says that the whole world cannot hold the books that were to be written.
