units.la: RESP. Primò Concedimus multa Dominum fecisse & dixisse, quæ non sunt scripta: sed quis nostrūm dicat, illa vel illa sunt? aut si dicere audeat, unde probat? Secundò pueriles sunt ineptiæ, captare amphibolias: nunquid enim Iohannes putavit libros á mundo tanquam locatum á loco capi nō posse? nequaquā: sed sensus hic est; non esset futurus in mundo quisquam, qui ea omnia animo capere & mente complecti posset præ varietate rerum gestarum ac multitudine & ex-cellentia. cellentia. Potuisset hoc Iesuita ex Glossa ordinaria cognoscere, quæ hæc verba sic explicat: Non dicit spacio non posse capi; sed capacitate legentium. Et ex Nicolao Lyrano, qui sic hunc locum explanat: Nec ipsum arbitror mundum, id est, homines huius mundi: Capere posse eos qui scriberentur libros. Facta enim & verba Christi nō sunt hominis tantum, sed Dei: quoniam illa humanitas erat organum divinitatis: & ideo non possunt ad plenum ab hominibus explicari aut etiam comprehendi. Et mox: Facta sunt & dicta Dei, quæ sunt nobis incomprehensibilia propter eorum excellentiam respectu intellectus nostri.
units.tr: ANSWER. First, we grant that the Lord did and said many things which are not written; but which of us says that these or those things are? Or if someone dares to say so, from what does he prove it? Second, it is childish to catch at ambiguities: did John think that the world could not hold books as if they were placed in a location? By no means; the sense is this: there would not be anyone in the world who could grasp in mind and embrace in thought all those things, on account of the variety of the deeds done and their multitude and excellence. The Jesuit could have learned this from the ordinary gloss, which explains these words thus: "It does not say that they cannot be contained by space, but by the capacity of the readers." And from Nicholas of Lyra, who explains this place thus: "Nor do I think the world itself, that is, the men of this world, could contain the books that would be written. For the deeds and words of Christ belong not only to a man but to God, since that humanity was the instrument of the divinity; and therefore they cannot be fully explained or even comprehended by men." And soon after: "The deeds and words of God are incomprehensible to us on account of their excellence with respect to our intellect."

units.la: Tertium testimonium.
units.tr: Third testimony.

units.la: Lucas testatur Act.1.3. Christum post resurrectionem per dies quadraginta discipulis apparuisse & locutum esse de regno Dei. At de gestis & verbis Domini post resurrectionem paucissima scripserunt Evangelistæ. Non autem est ullo modo credibile, Apostolos, qui illa viderant & audierant, non tradidisse Ecclesiis. nec enim invidi, aut obliviosi erat, ut nollent aut non possent ea dicere.
units.tr: Luke testifies in Acts 1:3 that Christ appeared to the disciples after the resurrection over forty days and spoke about the kingdom of God. But the Evangelists have written very little about the deeds and words of the Lord after the resurrection. Yet it is by no means credible that the Apostles, who had seen and heard those things, did not hand them down to the Churches; for it was not from envy or forgetfulness that they were unwilling or unable to tell them.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est: Si Christus post resurrectionem per dies quadraginta discipulis locutus est de regno Dei: & ea quae tum locutus est, non sunt omnia scripta, nihilominus tamen ab Apostolis tradita Ecclesiis; tum sunt traditiones non scriptæ. Omnia quæ antecedunt vera sunt: Ergo & quod sequitur.
units.tr: The syllogism is this: If Christ after the resurrection spoke with the disciples for forty days about the kingdom of God, and the things he then said are not all written, yet were nevertheless handed down by the Apostles to the Churches, then there are unwritten traditions. All the antecedents are true; therefore what follows.

units.la: RESP. Primo, in propositione est fallacia consequentis. Etsi enim totum antecedens concederetur, ex eo tamen nequaquam sequeretur, jam hoc tempore revera Apostolicas aliquas traditiones extare. Quis n. est tam vanus, tam temerarius, q[?] cū dixerit etiā vera, quibus voluerit & quæ voluerit, sine ullo testimonio divino affirmet ea esse, quæ Dominus per quadraginta dies post resurrectionem est locutus? Quis hoc nostrum faciet, & non maximam temeritatis culpam incurrat
units.tr: ANSWER. First, the premise contains the fallacy of the consequent. For even if the whole antecedent were granted, it would by no means follow from it that some Apostolic traditions actually exist at this time. For who is so vain and so rash that, having said even true things, whatever and whichever he pleases, he affirms without any divine testimony that these are the things which the Lord spoke during the forty days after the resurrection? Which of us will do this without incurring the greatest fault of rashness

units.la: in quo nec Prophetica nec Apostolica excellit autoritas ? Hæretici solent hoc argumento uti, & dicere, suas immunditias, esse ea quæ Christus post resurrectionem discipulis est locutus.
units.tr: in a matter in which neither prophetic nor apostolic authority excels? Heretics are accustomed to use this argument and to say that their own filthiness is what Christ spoke to the disciples after the resurrection.

units.la: Secundò, assumtionis tria sunt membra. Primum & tertium membrum est verum: medium vero, vid. quæ Christus locutus est, non esse omnia scripta: est ambiguum. Si enim intelligas, non esse omnia totidem verbis quæ à Domino usurpata sunt, conscripta; verum est: Sin autem intelligas, ne quidem summam eorum ad salutem necessariam esse scriptam; falsum est. Nam scriptum est licet summariè: tamen diserte & nominatim, quid Christus locutus sit, quid ve egerit: videl. dixit ea quæ ad regnum Dei pertinent Act. 1. 3. demonstravit se verè resurrexisse ex mortuis; jussitq; suam resurrectionem fratribus renunciare, eosq; in Galilæam abire, promisitq; sui ibi manifestationem Matth. 28. 9. 10. docuit oportuisse se pati & sic intrare in gloriam suam: & exorsus à Mose & omnibus Prophetis, interpretatus est illis in omnib. Scripturis, quæ de se scripta erat Luc. 24. 26. 27. revocavit eis in mentem quæ docuerat ante passionem suam, addens explicationem Scripturarū Luc. 24. 44. 45. 46. instituit ministerium Matth. 28. 29. promisit Spiritum Sanctum, & alia locutus est, & egit multa, quorum summa est ab Evangelistis conscripta.
units.tr: Second, the assumption has three parts. The first and third part is true; but the middle part, namely that what Christ spoke is not all written, is ambiguous. For if you understand that not all the words used by the Lord were written down word for word, it is true; but if you understand that not even the sum of what is necessary to salvation has been written, it is false. For although only in summary, yet plainly and by name, it is written what Christ said and did: namely, he spoke of the things that pertain to the kingdom of God, Acts 1. 3.; he demonstrated that he had truly risen from the dead, and ordered his resurrection to be announced to his brothers, and that they should go into Galilee, and promised his appearance there, Matth. 28. 9. 10.; he taught that it was necessary for him to suffer and so enter into his glory, and beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures what had been written about himself, Luke 24. 26. 27.; he recalled to their minds what he had taught before his passion, adding an explanation of the Scriptures, Luke 24. 44. 45. 46.; he instituted the ministry, Matth. 28. 29.; he promised the Holy Spirit; and he spoke and did many other things, the sum of which the Evangelists have written down.

units.la: Tertiò, quòd pauciora dicta & facta Christi post resurrectionem commemorantur, fit ideo, quia, ut Glossa ordinaria & Nicolaus Lyranus rectè annotant, non continuè per dies illos quadraginta, sed tamen frequenter discipulis apparuit.
units.tr: Third, that fewer sayings and deeds of Christ after the resurrection are recorded happens for this reason: as the ordinary gloss and Nicholas of Lyra rightly note, he did not appear continuously through those forty days, but nevertheless appeared often to the disciples.

units.la: Exceptio ad primam responsionis partem. De Sacramentorum institutione sine dubio Dominus tradidit in illis diebus quadraginta, quæ scripta non sunt.
units.tr: Objection to the first part of the answer. Without doubt the Lord handed down the institution of the sacraments in those forty days, and those teachings were not written down.

units.la: RESP. Primò, Si de Baptismo intelligas; scripta est illa traditio Matth. 28. 19. Profecti docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomen Patris & Filij & Spiritus Sancti. Sic Marc. 16. 16. Traditio Cænæ Domini etiam est scripta à Matthæo, Marco, Luca & Paulo. Aliorum Sacramentorum rum traditiones scriptæ non sunt, quia sine omni dubio de alys Sacramentis Dominus non tradidit quicquam. Secundo audacior est Iesuita, quám Glossa ordinaria & Nicolaus Lyranus, qui contenti narratione Lucæ, dicunt, Christum de Euangelio, Ecclesia, regno & beatitudine cælesti locutum: novorum autem Sacramentorum non meminerunt.
units.tr: Answer. First, if you mean Baptism, that tradition is written down in Matt. 28:19: "Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Likewise Mark 16:16. The tradition of the Lord's Supper is also written down by Matthew, Mark, Luke and Paul. The traditions of the other sacraments are not written down because, beyond all doubt, the Lord handed down nothing about the other sacraments. Second, the Jesuit is more daring than the Ordinary Gloss and Nicholas of Lyra, who, content with Luke's narrative, say that Christ spoke of the gospel, the Church, the kingdom and heavenly blessedness, but make no mention of new sacraments.

units.la: Quartum testimonium.
units.tr: The fourth testimony.

units.la: 1. Cor.11.2. ait Paulus: Laudo vero vos fratres, quòd omnia mea meministis, & sicut tradidi vobis, traditiones retinetis. Ergo sunt traditiones non scriptæ.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 11:2, where Paul says: "Now I praise you, brothers, that you remember me in all things and keep the traditions just as I delivered them to you." Therefore there are unwritten traditions.

units.la: RESPON. Plus colligitur, quàm antecedens permittit. Hoc enim tantùm sequitur, Apostolum tradidisse Corinthijs particulares de decore & honestate leges, ad Ecclesiasticam politiam spectantes: non autem hinc sequitur jam illas traditiones extare. Multò minus inde sequitur, illas traditiones quas Corinthijs Paulus tradidit esse Papisticas traditiones, cùm plerăq; Apostolorum doctrinæ maximè adversentur.
units.tr: Answer. More is inferred than the premise allows. For it follows only that the Apostle handed on to the Corinthians certain particular rules of decency and propriety, pertaining to the ecclesiastical polity; but it does not follow from this that those traditions now exist. Much less does it follow that the traditions which Paul handed on to the Corinthians are Papistical traditions, since for the most part they are very much opposed to the doctrine of the apostles.

units.la: Quintum testimonium.
units.tr: The fifth testimony.

units.la: 1. Cor.11.23. ait Paulus: Ego accepi à Domino, quod & tradidi vobis. Ergo sunt traditiones non scriptæ.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 11:23, where Paul says: "For I received from the Lord that which I also handed on to you." Therefore there are unwritten traditions.

units.la: RESP. Primò committitur elenchus allegati impertinentis testimonij. Nam dictum Pauli loquitur de traditione scripta institutione videlicet sacræ Cænæ, quam ibidem mox subjicit, at thesis probanda loquitur de traditionibus scriptis. Secundò prorsus aliud colligitur, quàm antecedens admittat. Non enim sequitur ex verbis Apostoli, esse traditiones non scriptas: verùm sacram Cænam non ab Apostolo excogitatam, sed à Domino ipso institutam esse.
units.tr: Answer. First, the argument commits the fallacy of citing an irrelevant testimony. For the words of Paul speak of a written tradition, namely the institution of the holy Supper, which he sets out right after in that same passage, whereas the thesis to be proved speaks of unwritten traditions. Second, something quite other is inferred than the premise admits. For it does not follow from the Apostle's words that there are unwritten traditions; rather, that the holy Supper was not devised by the Apostle but instituted by the Lord himself.

units.la: Sextum testimonium.
units.tr: The sixth testimony.

units.la: 1. Cor. 11. 34. ait Paulus: Cætera cùm venero, disponam. Quid autem disposuerit, nusquam scriptum invenitur.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 11:34, where Paul says: "The rest I will set in order when I come." What he set in order is nowhere found written.

units.la: Syllogismus erit talis: Si Paulus quædam apud Corinthios ordinavit, quæ nusquam scripta inveniuntur: tum sunt traditiones non scriptæ. Antecedens est verum: & consequens igitur.
units.tr: The syllogism will be this: If Paul ordained certain things among the Corinthians which are nowhere found written, then there are unwritten traditions. The antecedent is true, and so the consequent.

units.la: D
units.tr: D

units.la: RESPON. Primó sophisma est παρὰ τὸ ἑπόμενον in propositione connexa: quia etsi tunc cùm Paulus illa ordinaret apud Corinthios quæ pollicitus erat, fuerunt illæ traditiones non scriptæ: tamen non sequitur, jam quoq; illas exstare. Secundó committitur elenchus impertinentis testimonij. Nam Pauli testimonium non dicit, hac nostra ætate fore traditiones non scriptas: sed pollicetur saltem dispositionem eorum, quæ ad bonum ordinem in Ecclesia Corinthiaca seruandum pertinebant. Tertiò plus concludunt adversarij, quàm præmissæ patiuntur: nam etsi concederetur (quod tamen non conceditur) traditiones non scriptas de ceremoniis aliquibus ad bonum ordinem tuendum spectantibus ab Apostolo institutis exstare: tamen inde non sequeretur, etiam non scriptas traditiones dogmatum ad salutem necessariorum jam exstare: id quod volunt Papistæ.
units.tr: Answer. First, it is a sophism of the fallacy of the consequent [παρὰ τὸ ἑπόμενον] in a conditional proposition: for although, when Paul ordained those things among the Corinthians which he had promised, they were unwritten traditions, it still does not follow that they now exist. Second, the argument commits the fallacy of citing an irrelevant testimony. For the testimony of Paul does not say that in our own age there will be unwritten traditions; it only promises the arrangement of those things which pertained to keeping good order in the Corinthian church. Third, the opponents infer more than the premises allow: for even if it were granted (which is not granted) that unwritten traditions of certain ceremonies, instituted by the Apostle to preserve good order, exist, it would not follow from this that unwritten traditions of doctrines necessary to salvation now exist as well; and this is what the Papists want.

units.la: Exceptio. Merito censent Catholici Apostolum non solùm disposuisse quæ ad ritus & ceremonias pertinebant, sed etiā tradidisse alia graviora, ut de ordinatione ministrorū, de sacrificio altaris, de aliorum Sacramentorum forma & materia ; nec hæretici possunt ullo modo contrarium ostendere.
units.tr: Objection. Catholics rightly judge that the Apostle not only arranged the things pertaining to rites and ceremonies, but also handed on other, weightier matters, such as the ordination of ministers, the sacrifice of the altar, and the form and matter of the other sacraments; nor can the heretics in any way show the contrary.

units.la: RESPON. Primó merito censetur Iesuita principiū petere, qui asseverat tantum, non probat. Unde enim probabit, hac quæ enumerat, Apostolum disponere voluisse? Secundó dum pro traditionibus non scriptis Iesuita pugnat, ἀσύγκατα [?] scribit. Nam paulò ante fassus est, quid Apostolus disposuerit, nusquam scriptum inveniri, hic verò quid nā illud sit, quasi certò cognitum esset, commemorat. Tertiò petit principium dum asserit, Apostolum non tantum disposuisse, quæ ad ritus & ceremonias pertinebant, sed etiam alia graviora. Nam verbum διατάξομαι [?], ordinabo, quo Apostolus utitur, indicat, ea qualiacunq; fuerunt, ad ordinem Ecclesiasticum pertinuisse, non ad dogmata. Hæc enim est hujus verbi notatio propria: quod liquet ex simili loco 1. Cor. 16. 1. Parrò de collecollecta in sanctos, quemadmodum διέταξα[?], ordinavi ecclesijs Galatiae, ita & vos facite. Quod vero non etiam alia graviora se ordinaturum pollicitus est, potuisset Iesuita ex Thoma Aquinate discere, qui huc Apostoli locum ita explanat: Caetera scil. quae non sunt tanti periculi cum venero praesentialiter disponam, qualiter scilicet ea cōfervare debeatis. Quarto manifesta est antilogia, cum dicit, Apostolum non solum disposuisse, quae ad ritus & ceremonias pertinebant, sed etiam alia graviora: & tamen ea graviora quae enumerat, sunt ritus & ceremoniae. Quinto contradicit Scripturae: nam cum illa sacrificium altaris in Coena Domini non agnoscat, nec super altari, sed super mensa Dominus epulum illud sacrum instituerit: Iesuita cōtra nescio quod sacrificium altaris comminiscitur. Sexto, falsum est alia Sacramenta a Paulo fuisse Corinthijs tradita, quam quae DOMINUS instituit. Septimo, Sophistice mutat personam in disputando. Nam cum non possit probare, traditiones quas allegat, ab Apostolo Corinthijs commendatas esse, contra disputandi leges praeposterè[?] & iniquè nos contrarium ostendere jubet: cum aequius fuerit, ipsum, quod proposuit, idoneis argumentis probare. Nam opponenti incumbit probatio, non respondenti.
units.tr: Answer. First, the Jesuit is rightly judged to be begging the question, since he merely asserts and does not prove. For how will he prove that the Apostle wanted to arrange the things he lists? Second, while he fights for unwritten traditions, he writes incoherently [ἀσύγκατα]. For a little earlier he has admitted that what the Apostle ordained is nowhere found written, yet here he recounts what that was as if it were known for certain. Third, he begs the question when he asserts that the Apostle arranged not only the things pertaining to rites and ceremonies, but also other weightier matters. For the verb διατάξομαι [I will ordain], which the Apostle uses, indicates that whatever they were, they pertained to church order and not to doctrines. This is the proper meaning of this word, as is clear from a similar passage, 1 Cor. 16:1: Moreover, concerning the collection for the saints, as I ordained [διέταξα] to the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. That he did not promise to ordain other, weightier matters too, the Jesuit could have learned from Thomas Aquinas, who explains this passage of the Apostle as follows: "The rest, namely those which are not of such danger, I will set in order in person when I come, namely how you ought to keep them." Fourth, there is an obvious self-contradiction when he says that the Apostle arranged not only the things pertaining to rites and ceremonies but also other weightier matters, and yet the weightier matters he lists are rites and ceremonies. Fifth, he contradicts Scripture: for since Scripture recognizes no sacrifice of the altar in the Lord's Supper, and the Lord instituted that sacred feast not upon an altar but upon a table, the Jesuit invents I know not what sacrifice of the altar. Sixth, it is false that Paul handed on to the Corinthians any sacraments other than those the Lord instituted. Seventh, he sophistically shifts the burden in the disputation. For since he cannot prove that the traditions he cites were commended by the Apostle to the Corinthians, he orders us, contrary to the laws of disputation, to show the contrary, back to front and unfairly, when it would be more fitting for him to prove by suitable arguments what he has proposed. For the burden of proof lies on the one who opposes, not on the one who answers.

units.la: Septimum testimonium.
units.tr: The seventh testimony.

units.la: 2. Thessal. 2. 15. Itaq; fratres, tenete traditiones quas accepistis, sive per sermonem, sive per epistolam nostram.
units.tr: 2 Thess. 2. 15. So then, brethren, hold fast the traditions which you have been taught, whether by word or by our epistle.

units.la: Syllogismus est. Si sunt tenendae traditiones sive per sermonem sive per epistolam acceptae: tum sunt praeter Scripturam traditiones non scriptae. At illud est: Ergo & hoc.
units.tr: It is a syllogism. If traditions received either by word or by epistle are to be held, then there are unwritten traditions besides Scripture. But the first is so; therefore the second also.

units.la: RESPON. Primo est homonymia in nomine trad.tionis. Nam Apostolus nomine traditionum hic intelligit dogmata ad salutem necessaria, in quibus perstare & quae totis viribus retinere oportet omnes quicunq; salutem à Domino exspectant: at Iesuita intelligunt foetidissimas superstiti-tiones, tiones, quas imperitis hominibus obtrudunt. Secundò, nō est necessaria propositionis connexæ consequentia. Necessaria autem esset, si duo probare Iesuitæ possent: alterum, traditiones illas sermone à Paulo propositas, alias & prorsus diversas fuisse ab iis, quæ in epistolis continentur: secundò esse eas, quas Papistæ venditant. Sed unde utrumq; probabunt? Tertiò plus concluditur, quàm debet: nam hoc tantùm sequitur, vel cùm illam Epistolam Apostolus scriberet, tum nondum omnia dogmata scripta, ac ideo traditiones fuisse; non autem sequitur nunc traditiones esse: vel eandem doctrinam & viva voce & per epistolam ab Apostolo traditam fuisse.
units.tr: ANSWER. First, there is an equivocation in the word "tradition." For the Apostle here understands by traditions the doctrines necessary for salvation, which all who expect salvation from the Lord must persist in and hold fast with all their strength. But the Jesuits understand the most foul superstitions, which they foist upon ignorant people. Secondly, the consequence of the connected premise is not necessary. It would be necessary if the Jesuits could prove two things: first, that the traditions which Paul set forth by word were other and entirely different from those contained in the epistles; second, that they are those which the Papists peddle. But how will they prove either? Thirdly, more is concluded than should be. For only this follows: either that when he wrote that epistle the Apostle had not yet written down all doctrines, and so there were traditions at that time, but it does not follow that there are traditions now; or that the same doctrine was delivered by the Apostle both by living voice and by epistle.

units.la: I. Particula disjunctiva, sive, aperte indicat diversa esse quæ tradiderat & quæ scripserat.
units.tr: I. The disjunctive particle, "or," clearly indicates that what he delivered and what he wrote were different.

units.la: Syllogismus talis erit.
units.tr: The syllogism will be as follows.

units.la: Quandocunq; distributio constat disjunctiva particula sive, tum aliæ atq; aliæ res indicantur.
units.tr: Whenever a distribution is made with the disjunctive particle "or," then different things are indicated.

units.la: Atqui hæc distributio Paulina constat disjunctivâ particula sive:
units.tr: But this Pauline distribution is made with the disjunctive particle "or."

units.la: Ergo aliæ atq; aliæ res per eam indicantur.
units.tr: Therefore different things are indicated by it.

units.la: RESPON. Primo propositio est amphibola. Nā si per alias atq; alias res intelligantur diversi modi rei alicujus distributæ, vera est: sin autem intelligantur diversæ res distributæ, est falsa. Iam quàm hoc est frequentissimum, unam eandēq; rem diversis modis effici? ut cùm dicitur, eandem justificationis & regenerationis benedictionem significari credentibus, sive per Circumcisionem sive per baptismum: Eandem Christi communionem credentibus offerri, sive per Euangelium sive per Sacramenta. Nā diversi modi dādi vel accipiendi rem aliquam, non efficiunt rem ipsam diversam: ut eadē est fides, sive quæ confirmata fuit olim patribus per circumcisionem & Pascha, sive quæ nunc fidelibus confirmatur Baptismo & Cœna Domini. Idem est Christus, sive olim patribus per Sacrificia & figuras varias significatus, sive hodie nobis in Euangelio clarè demonstratus. Secundo, concedo quidem distributionem Paulinam constare particulâ disjunctivâ sive : sed illâ non indicantur diversæ traditiones, sed saltem diversi modi accipiendi easdem traditiones. Nam Apostolus non dicit, se alias traditiones per sermonem, alias per epistolam Thessalonicensibus commisisse : sed ostendit duntaxat duos distinctos modos, per quos Thessalonicenses easdē traditiones acceperant ; qui modi fuerunt, viva vox & epistola. Neq; modorum & instrumentorum diversitas rē diversam reddit : ut quis ferret ita argumentantem: Sive vivamus, sive moriamur, Domini sumus Ro. 14. 8. Ergo alterius sumus si vivamus, alterius si moriamur? Et 1. Cor. 15. 11. Sive igitur ego, sive illi ita prædicamus : Ergo aliud Euangelium prædicavit Paulus, aliud aliy Apostoli?
units.tr: ANSWER. First, the major premise is ambiguous. If by different things are meant different modes of one and the same distributed thing, it is true; but if different distributed things are meant, it is false. Now how very frequently is one and the same thing effected in diverse ways? As when it is said that the same blessing of justification and regeneration is signified to believers, whether through circumcision or through baptism; and that the same communion of Christ is offered to believers, whether through the Gospel or through the sacraments. For diverse modes of giving or receiving a thing do not make the thing itself different. Thus the faith is the same, whether it was once confirmed to the fathers through circumcision and the Passover, or is now confirmed to the faithful by Baptism and the Lord's Supper. Christ is the same, whether once signified to the fathers through sacrifices and various figures, or today clearly demonstrated to us in the Gospel. Secondly, I grant that the Pauline distribution is made with the disjunctive particle "or"; but by it are indicated not different traditions, but at least different modes of receiving the same traditions. For the Apostle does not say that he committed to the Thessalonians other traditions by word and others by epistle; he shows only two distinct modes by which the Thessalonians had received the same traditions, which modes were living voice and epistle. Nor does a diversity of modes and instruments make the thing diverse. Thus someone might bear with one arguing as follows: "Whether we live or die, we are the Lord's" (Rom. 14. 8). "Therefore we belong to one if we live, and to another if we die?" And (1 Cor. 15. 11): "Whether therefore I or they so preach." "Therefore Paul preached one gospel and the other apostles another?"

units.la: Exceptio 1. Si easdem traditiones & viva voce & per epistolam Thessalonicenses accepissent ; deberet epistola una ad Thessalonicenses continere omnem Euangelij doctrinam. Atqui posterius non est: Ergo nec prius.
units.tr: Exception 1. If the Thessalonians had received the same traditions both by living voice and by epistle, the one epistle to the Thessalonians ought to contain the whole doctrine of the Gospel. But the latter is not so; therefore neither is the former.

units.la: Probatio connexi: quia sine dubio totū Euangelium plenè illis prædicaverat, ut etiam colligitur ex cap. 1. & 2. prioris epistolæ.
units.tr: Proof of the connected premise: because without doubt he had fully preached the whole Gospel to them, as is also gathered from chapters 1 and 2 of the former epistle.

units.la: RESP. Nego propositionis connexæ consequentiam: & ad ejus probationem dico nihil facere citata testimonia: nam neq; in primo neq; in secundo capite id dicitur, quod Iesuita prætendit.
units.tr: ANSWER. I deny the consequence of the connected premise. As for its proof, I say that the cited testimonies do nothing for it: for neither in the first nor in the second chapter is that said which the Jesuit alleges.

units.la: Exceptio 2. Apostolus dicit in hoc ipso capite, se illis prædicasse de Antichristo, & præter alia docuisse, quando esset venturus : Et nunc, inquit, quid detineat scitis. Et, Num retinetis, quia cum essem vobiscum, hæc dicebam vobis? Hoc autem nusquam scriptum est, quando scilicet sit Antichristus venturus.
units.tr: Exception 2. The Apostle says in this very chapter that he had preached to them about Antichrist, and among other things had taught them when he would come: "And now," he says, "you know what restrains." And, "Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things?" But this is nowhere written, namely when Antichrist is to come.

units.la: RESPON: Primo, falsum est, Apostolum docuisse Thessalonicenses, quando Antichristus esset venturus. Deinde committitur elenchus allegationis impertinentium testimoniorum: Nam in testimonijs citatis non dicitur, Thessalonicēses scivisse quando Antichristus esset venturus: sed quid detineret, hoc est, quae fuerit causa morae ipsius, ut Glossa ordinaria & Lyranus declarat. Detinuit aut, quod tum Romani imperij vires adhuc integrae essent & non distractae: & quod Roma adhuc in plenaria potestate Romani Imperatoris esset. Illis autem verbis, Annon meministis me, cum adhuc essem apud vos, hoc dixisse vobis? multo minus significatur tempus adventus Antichristi: sed revocat Paulus Thessalonicensibus in memoriam, quid ipsis dixerit. quod vid. Antichristus venturus, qualis futurus, quid facturus esset?
units.tr: ANSWER: First, it is false that the Apostle taught the Thessalonians when Antichrist would come. Then the fallacy of alleging irrelevant testimonies is committed. For in the cited testimonies it is not said that the Thessalonians knew when Antichrist would come, but what restrains him, that is, what was the cause of his delay, as the Ordinary Gloss and Lyra explain. And what restrained him was that the powers of the Roman Empire were then still intact and undivided, and that Rome was still under the full power of the Roman Emperor. But by those words, "Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you this?" the time of Antichrist's coming is much less signified. Rather, Paul reminds the Thessalonians of what he had told them: that Antichrist would come, what sort of man he would be, and what he would do.

units.la: Octavum testimonium.
units.tr: The eighth testimony.

units.la: 1. Timoth. 6. 20. dicitur, O Timothee depositum custodi. Syllogismus talis erit: Si Timotheus debet custodire depositum: ergo jam exstant traditiones non scriptae. Antecedens est: Ergo & consequens.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 6.20 says, "O Timothy, guard the deposit." The syllogism will be this: If Timothy must keep the deposit, then unwritten traditions already exist. The antecedent holds; therefore the consequent holds too.

units.la: RESP. Primo nulla est propositionis consequentia, cum ea connectantur, quorum alterum ex altero conditione non consequitur. Secundo per depositum non intelligitur traditiones non scriptae: sed sana Euangelij doctrina, & dona quaecunq; ad Ecclesiae aedificationem, veluti depositum, Deus comiserat Timotheo: Sicut & Thomas Aquinas in explanatione hujus loci ait: Depositum hominis est omne bonum, quod habet quilibet, quod sibi commissum est a Deo ut conservet & multiplicet. 1.Cor.15. Et gratia ejus in me vacua non fuit. Et sic dicit ei, ut depositum custodiat, id est, ut se in gratia Dei conservet & multiplicet. Et specialiter praelati habent depositum, scilicet cura proximorum & fidelium. Ioh.ult. Pasce oves meas. Hebr. ult. Ipsi pervigilant quasi rationem reddituri pro animabus vestris. Similiter Nicolaus Lyranus per depositum intelligit gregem Timothei fidelitati commissum. Iesuiigitur per depositum traditiones non scriptas intelligens & ab Apostoli sensu & ab aliorum Catholicorum interpretatione dissentit.
units.tr: RESP. Firstly, there is no consequence in the proposition, since the things joined together are such that one does not follow from the other on that condition. Secondly, by "deposit" is not meant unwritten traditions, but the sound doctrine of the Gospel and all the gifts that God entrusted to Timothy for the building up of the Church, as a deposit. Thomas Aquinas also says in his explanation of this passage: "The deposit of a man is every good that anyone has, which has been committed to him by God to keep and to increase. 1 Cor. 15: 'And his grace towards me was not in vain.' So he tells him to guard the deposit, that is, to keep and increase himself in the grace of God. Prelates in particular hold a deposit, namely the care of their neighbours and the faithful. John 21: 'Feed my sheep.' Heb. 13: 'They watch as those who must give account for your souls.'" Likewise Nicholas of Lyra understands by "deposit" the flock committed to Timothy's faithfulness. The Jesuit, therefore, by understanding unwritten traditions as the deposit, departs both from the Apostle's meaning and from the interpretation of other Catholics.

units.la: Tertió, calumniam committit Iesuita, dum nobis impingit, ac si depositum de libris scriptis seu membranis aut chartis quibus Verbum Dei inscriptum est, interpretaremur: aliud enim per depositum intelligimus, quàm membranas vel chartas. Ac propterea etiam vanus est & puerilis lusus, cum subjicit: Si loqueretur de verbis scriptis, nō tam anxiē commendaret depositū: Scripturæ enim facilè conservantur in thecis & á librarijs. Quasi verò putaremus, Apostolum sollicitum fuisse, ne Timotheus membranas aut librum incuria quadam amitteret, ut negligentes scholastici solent. O subtiles Iesuitæ conjecturas!
units.tr: Thirdly, the Jesuit commits a calumny when he charges us with interpreting the deposit as books written on parchment or paper on which the Word of God is inscribed. For we understand something other by the deposit than parchment or paper. And therefore his petty and childish play is empty too, when he adds: "If he were speaking of written words, he would not commend the deposit so anxiously, for Scriptures are easily kept in cases and by booksellers." As if we supposed the Apostle was anxious lest Timothy should lose through some carelessness the parchments or a book, as careless schoolboys tend to do. O subtle Jesuit conjectures!

units.la: Nonum testimonium.
units.tr: The ninth testimony.

units.la: 2. Tim. 1.13.14. Formam habe sanorum verborum, quæ à me audisti. Bonum depositum custodi per Spiritum Sanctum, qui habitat in nobis.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 1.13, 14: "Hold the form of sound words, which you have heard from me. Keep the good deposit through the Holy Spirit, who dwells in us."

units.la: Syllogismus talis erit: Si minister Ecclesiæ habere debet formam sanorum verborum, ab Apostolo auditorū: eaq; tanquam bonum depositum custodienda per Spiritum Sanctum, qui habitat in nobis; tum sunt traditiones non scriptæ. Quæ antecedunt vera sunt omnia: Ergo & quod sequitur.
units.tr: The syllogism will be this: If a minister of the Church must hold the form of sound words which he heard from the Apostle, and must keep them as a good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us, then there are unwritten traditions. All the antecedents are true; therefore the consequent is too.

units.la: RESP. Primò, Fallit connexum sophismate πως[?] τὸ ἐπόμενον[?]. Nam dictum Apostoli non loquitur de traditionibus non scriptis: sed de forma sanorum verborum & præclaro depositò, hoc est, de sincera Euangelij doctrina, quam à Paulo audiverat Timotheus, & de præclaris illis donis, quæ Deus tanquam talentum in usum Ecclesiæ conferendum Timotheo commiserat.
units.tr: RESP. Firstly, the inference is fallacious, through the fallacy of the consequent. For the Apostle's saying does not speak of unwritten traditions, but of the form of sound words and of the excellent deposit, that is, of the sincere doctrine of the Gospel, which Timothy had heard from Paul, and of those excellent gifts which God had entrusted to Timothy as a talent to be employed for the Church.

units.la: Secundò, admittit Iesuita calumniam, dum testimonium Apostoli truncat, dissimulatis ijs quæ tegi nequaquam debebant. Omisit enim hæc verba, in fide & charitate, quæ est in Christo Iesu. At cur omisit? quia sententiam ipsius evertebant. Nam cùm sana doctrina duo capita Apostolus statuat, fidem & charitatem, quæ est in Christo Iesu: utrumq; perfectè in Scriptura traditur: ita ut ex traditionibus quicquā adjici necesse non sit. Nam si fidem spectes, ea scripta sunt, quæ credetes vitam æternã habeamus per nomen Christi. Joh.20.31. Hæc autem scripta sunt, ut credatis Jesum esse Christum illum, Filium illum Dei, & ut credentes vitam habeatis per nomen ejus. Ergo nulla, non scripta traditio de fide, ad salutem est necessaria.
units.tr: Secondly, the Jesuit admits a calumny when he truncates the Apostle's testimony, passing over words that by no means ought to have been hidden. For he omitted these words: "in faith and love, which is in Christ Jesus." But why did he omit them? Because they overturn his opinion. For since the Apostle sets down two heads of sound doctrine, faith and love, which is in Christ Jesus, both are fully delivered in Scripture, so that nothing need be added from traditions. For if you look at faith, these things are written, "that believing you may have life through his name" (John 20.31). But these things are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, that Son of God, and that believing you may have life through his name. Therefore no unwritten tradition concerning faith is necessary for salvation.

units.la: Sin vero charitatis doctrinam intueamur, ea quoq; perfectè in Scriptura traditur: nam tota charitatis Summa duobus illis mandatis tota comprehenditur: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo & ex tota anima tua & ex tota cogitatione tua. Istud est primum & magnum mandatum. Secundum autem simile est huc: Diliges proximum tuum ut teipsum. Ab iis duobus mandatis TOTA Lex & Prophetæ pendent. Matth.22.37.38.39.40.
units.tr: But if we look at the doctrine of love, this too is fully delivered in Scripture, for the whole sum of love is comprehended in those two commandments: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets." Matt. 22.37, 38, 39, 40.

units.la: Decimum testimonium.
units.tr: The tenth testimony.

units.la: 2.Tim.2.1. Tu ergo, fili mi, confortare in gratia quæ est in Christo Jesu: & quæ audisti á me per multos testes, hæc commenda fidelibus hominibus, qui idonei erunt & alios docere. Non loquitur de verbis scriptis: nam alioquin non adderet; Hæc commenda fidelibus, qui idonei erunt & alios docere. sed diceret, commenda librarijs, ut multa exempla transcribant. Nec diceret; Quæ audisti á me per multos testes, sed, quæ scripsi tibi. Itaq; non verba solum, sed etiam sensum, ac multo magis hunc, quàm illa Timotheo Apostolus commendat, ac ut per manus tradat successoribus [?] suis jubet.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 2.1. "You therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. And the things you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit these to faithful men, who will be able to teach others." He is not speaking of written words, for otherwise he would not add: "Commit these to faithful men who will be able to teach others," but would say, "Commit them to scribes, so that they may copy out many examples." Nor would he say, "the things you have heard from me among many witnesses," but "the things I have written to you." Therefore the Apostle commends to Timothy not only the words but also the sense, and much more the sense than the words, and orders that it be handed on by hand to his successors.

units.la: Syllogismus est talis: Si audita ab Apostolo fuerunt commendata fidelibus hominibus, qui essent idonei ad alios quoq; docendos: tum certè sunt traditiones non scriptæ. Aliqui prius est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: The syllogism is this: If things heard from the Apostle were committed to faithful men who would be fit to teach others also, then there certainly are unwritten traditions. The antecedent is true; therefore the consequent is too.

units.la: RESP. Primò in propositione est fallacia consequentis: quia audita possunt esse scripta. Cujus rei evidens est testimonium Act.17.11. Nam quæ Beræenses audiverant á Paulo, eadem in Scripturis repererunt. Qualis igitur est hæc consequentia: Audita sunt: ergo scripta non sunt?
units.tr: RESP. Firstly, in the proposition there is the fallacy of the consequent, because things heard may also be written. Of this the clear proof is Acts 17.11. For what the Bereans had heard from Paul, they found the same in the Scriptures. What kind of inference, then, is this: "They were heard; therefore they were not written"?

units.la: Secundò differtit Iesuita à Thoma Aquinate magistro suo, qui ex hoc loco Pauli nullas traditiones non scriptas collegit, sed eum ita explanauit, ut satis appareat, eum audita illa intellexisse de doctrina Euangelij Propheticis scriptis confirmata. Sic enim ait Aquinas: Monet eum, ut si ad martyrium venerit, ut dispenset doctrinam fidei. Paulo post: Quae audisti à me & ego à Christo: & dico à me non singulariter, sed confirmata per multos testes, id est, per legem & Prophetas. Rom 3. Testificata à lege & Prophetis: vel per Apostolos 1. Cor.15. Sive enim ego, sive illi sic praedicamus & sic credidistis.
units.tr: Secondly, the Jesuit differs from his teacher Thomas Aquinas, who from this passage of Paul gathered no unwritten traditions, but explained it in such a way that it clearly appears he understood those things heard as the doctrine of the Gospel confirmed by the prophetic writings. For Aquinas says: "He warns him that if he comes to martyrdom, he should dispense the doctrine of the faith." A little later: "The things you have heard from me and I from Christ: and I say from me not singly, but confirmed by many witnesses, that is, by the Law and the Prophets." Rom. 3. Attested by the Law and the Prophets; or by the Apostles, 1 Cor. 15: "For whether I or they, so we preach and so you have believed."

units.la: Exceptio. 1. Si innueret Apostolus doctrinam fidei quae ipsius scriptis est comprehensa; tum non dixisset, commenda fidelibus hominibus, sed commenda librarijs, ut multa exempla transscribant. Atqui dixit, Commenda fidelibus, & non, commenda librarijs, ut multa exempla transscribant: Igitur non innuit Apostolus doctrinam fidei quae ipsius scriptis est comprehensa.
units.tr: Objection 1. If the Apostle hinted at a doctrine of the faith that is comprehended in his writings, he would not have said, "commit to faithful men," but "commit to scribes, so that they may copy out many examples." But he said, "Commit to faithful men," and not "commit to scribes, so that they may copy out many examples." Therefore the Apostle did not hint at a doctrine of the faith comprehended in his writings.

units.la: RESP. Primò propositio est falsa. Cui enim sano persuadebitur, quae commendanda sunt fidelibus hominibus ad docendum, ea non esse scripta? Vetus & novum testamentum commendandum est diligenter fidelibus hominibus qui apti sint ad docendum alios: Nunquid igitur Vetus & novum testamentum scriptum non est? Secundò mutatur status quaestionis usitatâ Bellarmino Sophisticâ: non enim dicimus, Apostolo curae fuisse, ut multa exemplaria Scripturae haberetur, ut falsò innuit Iesuita: Sed doctrinā illam fidelib. comendādā hominibus, nō fuisse aliam, quàm quae Scripturis continetur.
units.tr: RESP. Firstly, the proposition is false. For who in his right mind would be persuaded that the things which are to be committed to faithful men for teaching are not written? The Old and New Testament is to be committed diligently to faithful men who are fit to teach others. Is the Old and New Testament, then, not written? Secondly, the state of the question is altered by the sophistry customary with Bellarmine. For we do not say that it was the Apostle's concern that many copies of Scripture should be kept, as the Jesuit falsely hints; but that the doctrine to be committed to faithful men was no other than that which is contained in the Scriptures.

units.la: Exceptio. 2. Si doctrinam scriptam Apostolus intelligeret, non diceret, Quae audisti, sed, quae scripsi tibi. At dixit, quae audisti, non autem, quae scripsi tibi: Ergo doctrinam scriptam Apostolus non intelligit.
units.tr: Objection 2. If the Apostle meant written doctrine, he would not have said, "the things you have heard," but "the things I have written to you." But he said, "the things you have heard," and not "the things I have written to you." Therefore the Apostle does not mean written doctrine.

units.la: RESP. Connexum non est necessariae veritatis: quia audita possunt esse scripta. Audimus in templis doctrinam Euan
units.tr: RESP. The connection is not of necessary truth, because things heard may also be written. We hear the doctrine of the Gospel in churches

units.la: E gelij: gelij : num igitur illa scripta non est ? Imo ex Scriptura recitatam audimus. Nam auditum esse & scriptum esse non sunt opposita, cúm simul esse possint.
units.tr: The doctrine of the Gospel: is it therefore not written? Indeed, we hear it read out from Scripture. For to have been heard and to have been written are not opposites, since they can both be the case at once.

units.la: Vltimum testimonium.
units.tr: The last testimony.

units.la: In 2.& 3. epistola Iohannes dicit: Multa habens scribere vobis, nolui per chartam & atramentum, &c. Ex his intelligimus, multa ab Apostolo Iohanne dicta esse discipulis, & per discipulos Ecclesia universa, quae tamen scripta non sunt.
units.tr: In the second and third epistles John says: "Having many things to write to you, I was unwilling to do so with paper and ink," etc. From these words we understand that the apostle John told many things to his disciples, and through the disciples to the whole Church, which nevertheless were not written down.

units.la: Syllogismus hujusmodi fuerit:
units.tr: The syllogism would be of this kind:

units.la: Si Iohannes & alij discipuli multa dixerunt, quae tamen scripta non sunt: tum sunt traditiones non scriptae. Antecedens est verum, ut patet ex allegatis testimonijs. Ergo & consequens verum est.
units.tr: If John and the other disciples said many things that were nevertheless not written down, then there are unwritten traditions. The antecedent is true, as is clear from the testimonies cited. Therefore the consequent is also true.

units.la: RESP. Primò assumtum est ambiguum. Nam si intelliguntur quae scripta non sunt, scil. totidem expressis verbis quibus sunt proposita ab Apostolis, est verum: neque nos asseveramus, omnia omninò verba ab Apostolis prolata, esse conscripta: sed omnia dogmata ad salutem necessaria Scripturâ Sacrâ esse comprehensa dicimus. Sin autem intelligatur assumtum etiam de dogmatibus ipsis, videl. ea quoque omnia scripta non exstare, falsum est. Omnia enim dogmata ad salutem necessaria sacris literis continentur: quia Sacrae literae possunt hominem sapientem reddere ad salutem, ut testatur Paulus 2. Tim. 3. 15. Secundò allegantur ad probationem assumtionis testimonia impertinentia. Nam testimonia illa in 2. & 3. Iohan loquuntur saltem de brevibus illis Iohannis epistolis: at assumtio etiam de aliorum Apostolorum scriptis. Videte igitur, qualis sit argumentatio: In duabus epistolis Iohannis non sunt omnia scripta : Ergo in Sacra Scriptura non sunt omnia scripta ? Atqui Sophisticum est, negato uno membro, integrum negare. Ac perinde est ac si quis ita argumentaretur: Ille homo non habet digitum : Ergo non habet corpus. vel: Hominis aures duae non moventur: ergo corpus non movetur. Tertió plus concluditur, quàm legitilegitime potest. Nam non sequitur, si Iohannes multa noluit scribere in duabus illis epistolis; esse nunc traditiones non scriptas: sed hoc saltem sequitur, Apostolum multa in adventum suum distulisse, quæ coram exponeret. Illa autem multa, fuerunt necessaria dogmata de Christo salutis autore, cujus Euangelium solidam lætitiam auditoribus affert: talia enim fuisse quæ coram Iohannes declarare voluit, cōtextus indicat. Non fuerunt autem traditiones de rebus inanibus & ridiculis ceremoniis: nam ex his gaudium nostrum non fit completum.
units.tr: ANSWER. First, the assumption is ambiguous. For if it is understood as referring to things that are not written, namely not in exactly the words in which they were uttered by the apostles, it is true. Nor do we assert that every word spoken by the apostles was committed to writing; we say that all doctrines necessary to salvation are comprehended in Holy Scripture. But if the assumption is understood as also concerning the doctrines themselves, namely that these too are not all extant in writing, it is false. For all doctrines necessary to salvation are contained in the holy letters, because the holy letters can make a man wise unto salvation, as Paul testifies, 2 Tim. 3.15. Secondly, the testimonies alleged in proof of the assumption are irrelevant. For those testimonies in 2 and 3 John speak at least of those short epistles of John, but the assumption concerns also the writings of the other apostles. See, then, what kind of argument this is: In two epistles of John not everything is written; therefore in Holy Scripture not everything is written? But it is a sophism, when one member is denied, to deny the whole. It is just as if someone argued thus: That man has no finger; therefore he has no body. Or: The two ears of a man are not moved; therefore the body is not moved. Thirdly, more is concluded than can legitimately be concluded. For it does not follow that, if John was unwilling to write many things in those two epistles, there are now unwritten traditions; but only this follows, that the apostle deferred many things until his coming, which he would explain in person. Those many things, however, were the necessary doctrines concerning Christ, the author of salvation, whose gospel brings solid joy to its hearers; for the context indicates that such were the things John wished to declare in person. But they were not traditions about empty matters and ridiculous ceremonies, for our joy is not made complete by these.

units.la: Deniq; prorsus aliud colligitur & principium manifestè petitur, cum impudeter asseritur, Traditiones Papisticas esse ea, quæ Iohannes in duabus illis brevibus epistolis nō scripsit.
units.tr: Finally, something quite different is inferred, and the principle is plainly begged when it is shamelessly asserted that the Papistical traditions are those things which John did not write in those two short epistles.

units.la: Hæc sunt omnia Scripturæ testimonia á Bellarmino citata, quæ nonsolùm nonjuvant, sed etiam sententiâ ipsius lædunt.
units.tr: These are all the testimonies of Scripture cited by Bellarmine, which not only do not help him but even harm his own position.

units.la: Ac proinde manet firma & inconcussa thesis supra posita: Apostolicas traditiones non scriptas, de quibus certò cognitum sit, quòd ab Apostolis sint traditæ, nunc nullas esse. ὅπερ ἔδει ὑπερασπίσαι[?]
units.tr: And so the firm and unshaken thesis set forth above remains: that apostolic unwritten traditions, of which it is known with certainty that they were handed down by the apostles, do not exist now. ὅπερ ἔδει ὑπερασπίσαι[?]

units.la: ET HACTENUS DE TRADITIONE DI- VINA: sequitur de humana.
units.tr: SO MUCH CONCERNING DIVINE TRADITION; there follows the discussion of human tradition.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Traditio humana, est quæ ab hominibus ex humano consilio est profecta.
units.tr: Human tradition is that which has proceeded from men by human counsel.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Eaq; vel pia est vel impia.
units.tr: And this is either pious or impious.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Traditio pia, est quæ cum Scriptura Prophetica & Apostolica congruit.
units.tr: A pious tradition is that which agrees with the prophetic and apostolic Scripture.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Cujus generis sunt probati legitimorum conciliorum Canones: & bene constitutarum Ecclesiarum ordinationes.
units.tr: Of this kind are the approved canons of lawful councils, and the ordinances of well-established congregations.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Traditio impia, est quæ cum Scriptura Prophetica & Apostolica pugnat.
units.tr: An impious tradition is that which fights against the prophetic and apostolic Scripture.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: Qualis taxatur á Christo Matth.15.3. Quare & vos trāsgredimini mandatum Dei per traditionem vestram?
units.tr: Such as is censured by Christ, Matt. 15.3: "Why do you also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?"

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Ejusmodi traditiones sunt pleraq; Cabalistica, quae Iudaeis primum ore tradita & tandem ab insanis hominibus in blasphemos Thalmudis libros sunt relata.
units.tr: Most traditions of this kind are Cabalistic, which were first handed down orally to the Jews and at last were carried by mad men into the blasphemous books of the Talmud.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Rursus humana traditio vel utilis est vel inutilis.
units.tr: Again, human tradition is either useful or useless.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Utilis traditio, est quae ad aedificationem Ecclesiae facit: ut qualis ordo & disciplina in Ecclesia servanda: quibus horis ad audiendas sacras conciones vel ad celebranda Sacramenta populo sit conveniendum: quali exhortatione ante administrationem Sacramentorum ad populum utendum: qualis precum formula usurpanda, &c.
units.tr: A useful tradition is that which contributes to the edification of the Church: such as what order and discipline is to be kept in the Church; at what hours the people are to assemble for hearing sacred sermons or for celebrating the sacraments; what exhortation is to be given to the people before the administration of the sacraments; what form of prayer is to be used, etc.

units.la: XXXIIX.
units.tr: XXXIIX.

units.la: Inutilis traditio, est quae citra aedificationem pietatis instituitur.
units.tr: A useless tradition is that which is instituted without any edification of piety.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Piae & utiles traditiones, quae ad tranquillitatem & bonum ordinem in Ecclesia conducunt, sunt servanda.
units.tr: Pious and useful traditions, which lead to tranquillity and good order in the Church, are to be kept.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Earum tamen observatio non est justitia coram Deo; nec est cultus Dei: nec meretur remissionem peccatorum.
units.tr: Their observance, however, is not righteousness before God, nor is it worship of God, nor does it merit the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: XLI.
units.tr: XLI.

units.la: Suntq; illae traditiones res adiaphorae, quae extra casum scandali omitti possint.
units.tr: And those traditions are things indifferent (adiaphora), which may be omitted outside the case of scandal.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Sed illi peccant, qui cum scandalo eas violant, & suarum Ecclesiarum tranquillitatem temere perturbant.
units.tr: But those sin who violate them with scandal and rashly disturb the tranquillity of their own congregations.

units.la: XLIII.
units.tr: XLIII.

units.la: Gravius vero illi peccant, qui eas observant cum opinione necessitatis, cultus Dei & meriti.
units.tr: More gravely, however, sin those who observe them with the opinion that they are necessary, as worship of God and as meriting something.

units.la: HUC USQUE IN GENERE DE TRADI- TIONIBUS: sequitur jam in specie de tradi- tionibus Papisticis.
units.tr: So far in general about traditions; now follows in particular the Papistical traditions.

units.la: XLIV.
units.tr: XLIV.

units.la: Papisticæ traditiones, sunt humanæ constitutiones, quæ in Papatu præter & contra Sacram Scripturā sunt receptæ.
units.tr: Papistical traditions are human constitutions which have been received in the Papacy besides and against Holy Scripture.

units.la: XLV.
units.tr: XLV.

units.la: Illa non sunt Apostolica.
units.tr: They are not apostolic.

units.la: XLVI.
units.tr: XLVI.

units.la: Nec sunt Propheticis vel Apostolicis [?] traditionibus exaquanda.
units.tr: Nor are they to be equated with prophetic or apostolic traditions.

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Nec sunt Spirituales seu ad animam pertinentes.
units.tr: Nor are they spiritual or pertaining to the soul.

units.la: XLIIX.
units.tr: XLIIX.

units.la: Nec sunt ad vitam æternam necessariæ.
units.tr: Nor are they necessary to eternal life.

units.la: XLIX.
units.tr: XLIX.

units.la: Nec debent nec possunt feré ulla bona cōscientiā observari.
units.tr: Nor can or should they almost ever be observed with a good conscience.

units.la: L.
units.tr: L.

units.la: 1. Quia sunt laquei ad strangulandas miseras animas: sunt crudelis carnificina animarum. Nam tantus est earum acervus, tanta earū difficultas, ut fieri non possit, quin extrema anxietate & terrore perplexi urantur, quibus moles earum & stricta observatio incumbit.
units.tr: 1. Because they are snares for strangling wretched souls; they are a cruel butchery of souls. For their heap is so great and their difficulty so great that it cannot but happen that those on whom their burden and strict observance rest are tormented, perplexed with extreme anxiety and terror.

units.la: LI.
units.tr: LI.

units.la: 2. quia propter ipsas irritum fit præceptum Dei.
units.tr: 2. Because on account of them the command of God is made void.

units.la: LII.
units.tr: LII.

units.la: 3. quia Deum ipsum qui unicus est Ecclesiæ Legislator, suo jure spoliant.
units.tr: 3. Because they strip God himself, who alone is the Lawgiver of the Church, of his right.

units.la: LIII.
units.tr: LIII.

units.la: 4. quia regnum Christi destruunt.
units.tr: 4. Because they destroy the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: LIV.
units.tr: LIV.

units.la: 5. quia libertatem Christianam, á Christo fidelium conscientiis datam, penitus opprimunt.
units.tr: 5. Because they utterly oppress the Christian liberty given by Christ to the consciences of the faithful.

units.la: LV.
units.tr: LV.

units.la: 6. quia ex ipsis peccatorum remissionem, gratiam & placationem Dei, satisfactionem pro peccatis, justitiam & salutem aeternam quaerere docent cum summa meriti Christi injuria.
units.tr: 6. Because from them they teach that forgiveness of sins, the grace and propitiation of God, satisfaction for sins, and righteousness and eternal salvation are to be sought, to the great injury of the merit of Christ.

units.la: LVI.
units.tr: LVI.

units.la: 7. quia pro vero Dei cultu sacrilegè habentur & obtrunduntur.
units.tr: 7. Because they are sacrilegiously held and pressed forward as the true worship of God.

units.la: LVII.
units.tr: LVII.

units.la: 8. quia impiè aeternae mortis denunciatione sunt sancua[?].
units.tr: 8. Because they are impiously sanctioned by the threat of eternal death.

units.la: LIIX.
units.tr: LIIX.

units.la: 9. quia falsò exiguntur tanquam ad salutem aeternam necessaria.
units.tr: 9. Because they are falsely demanded as necessary to eternal salvation.

units.la: LIX.
units.tr: LIX.

units.la: 10. quia sunt inutiles.
units.tr: 10. Because they are useless.

units.la: LX.
units.tr: LX.

units.la: 11. quia Iudaismum & Gentilismū invehunt, ac proinde Samaritanismum, hoc est, variarum religionum mixturam.
units.tr: 11. Because they introduce Judaism and paganism, and consequently Samaritanism, that is, a mixture of various religions.

units.la: LXI.
units.tr: LXI.

units.la: 12. quia sunt ad foedum quaestum prostituta.
units.tr: 12. Because they are prostituted for a shameful profit.

units.la: LXII.
units.tr: LXII.

units.la: 13. quia earum observationem sequuntur horrenda Dei judicia. Iesa.29.19.
units.tr: 13. Because the observance of them is followed by dreadful judgements of God. Isa. 29.19.

units.la: LXIII.
units.tr: LXIII.

units.la: 14. quia cùm sint perversa hominum inventa, Deo in religionis causa displicent. Matth.15.9.
units.tr: 14. Because, since they are perverse inventions of men, they displease God in matters of religion. Matt. 15.9.

units.la: LXIV.
units.tr: LXIV.

units.la: 15. quia partim sunt impia, partim nugatoria.
units.tr: 15. Because some are impious, others trifling.

units.la: LXV.
units.tr: LXV.

units.la: Ex quo genere sunt, ut ex infinitis paucas quasdam exempli causa commemoremus, quibus praecipiuntur
units.tr: Of this kind are, to mention a few out of countless examples, those which are commanded, such as:

units.la: Adorationes[?] imaginum & statuarum atq; adeo idolorum.
units.tr: The adorations of images and statues, and indeed of idols.

units.la: Agnus Dei qui ex cera conficitur, adhibitis certis praeculis, cui tribuunt eandem vim divinam, quae ipsi Filio Dei, qui verè veré est Agnus Dei, tribuitur: qua de re exstant vulgati ver-sus, plenissimi impietatis: Lib.1. Ceremoniarum Curia Romanæ tit 7. in fine.
units.tr: The Agnus Dei, which is made from wax, with certain prayers added, to which they ascribe the same divine power that is ascribed to the Son of God himself, who truly is the Lamb of God. Concerning this there exist common verses, most full of impiety: Book 1 of the Ceremonies of the Roman Curia, title 7, at the end.

units.la: Balsamus, & munda cera, cum chrismatis unda, Conficiunt agnum, quod manus do tibi magnum Fonte velut natum, per mystica sanctificatum. Fulgura desursum depellit, & omne malignum Peccatum frangit, ut Christi sanguis, & angit, Prægnans servatur, simul & partus liberatur, Munera fert dignis, virtutem destruit ignis, Portatus mundé, de fluctibus eripit undæ.
units.tr: Balsam and pure wax, with the water of chrism, they make a lamb, which I give to you as something great, born as it were from the font, sanctified by mystical rites. It drives away lightning from above and breaks every evil sin, as the blood of Christ does, and it strangles; the pregnant woman is kept safe and at the same time her child is freed; it bears gifts to the worthy, it destroys the power of fire, carried cleanly, it snatches from the waves of the sea.

units.tr: It is written, moreover, that Pope Urban V sent three Lambs of God with these verses to the Emperor of the Greeks. The procession of the ass crowned with palms. Altars, on which Masses are celebrated and sacrifices offered. Acolytes, or more correctly Acolouthoi. Ave Maria. Albs and other linen choir vestments. Holy water, or consecrated water. The aspergillum. The washing of feet on the day of the Lord's Supper, the day before Parasceve. The washing of altars. Abstinence from meat on forbidden days. Baths of souls, which are heated for the poor for the sake of refreshing souls in purgatory. Blessings of cakes. Consecrations of images and tombs. Baptisms of bells, with godfathers or sponsors present. Distinctions and choices of foods. Consecration and anointing of priests and little priests. Chrism, or the anointing of infants in baptism and of adults in confirmation. Chasuble; candelabra; consecrated candles and lamps. Ciborium, or repository, or case, in which is kept the god Maozim, or the all-healing god, who is carried about in a Persian procession. Little bells, cymbals, handbells and rattles. Consecrated ashes and the receiving of consecrated ashes. Auricular confession, which is made to the priest in the ear. The Lord's Supper under one kind. The rocking of the cradle of Christ. Carnival. The taper-bearer. The cross to be laid in the sepulchre of the Lord. Consecrations of fire; consecration of the Paschal candle. Wooden doves let down from on high on the day of Pentecost. The seventh and thirtieth-day anniversaries. Dedications of altars. Days of the cross, or religious processions. Countless feast days, commanded under penalty of excommunication and due obedience. Exorcism. Fraternities. The feast of the body of Christ, in which the idol Maozim is carried about in a theatrical procession. The Veronica face. The figure of the cross to be made with the fingers over the forehead and breast. The canonical hours. Consecrated herbs, by which evil demons are put to flight. Images of the cross of indulgences; and other images, such as of the saints and especially of the blessed Virgin Mary, the Redemptrix and Saviouress. Invocations of dead saints. Little images of the saints, wrapped in cloths through Lent, or baubles. Markets of indulgences. The image of the cross which is called the Agnus Dei, of which above; the beginning of the Gospel of St John, enclosed in certain slips and hung from the neck. The Lenten fast. The doorkeeper. Readers of the Gospel and Epistles in the Mass. Lamps, flasks and torches. The litany by which the saints are invoked. Private Masses, which are said at every corner of the churches, for the living and the dead. The Mass of the crown of thorns. The Mass of the three nails. The Mass of the foreskin of Christ. The Mass for those sailing. The Mass for those travelling on horse or on foot. The Mass for pregnant women. The Mass for women in labour. The Mass for barren women. The Mass for those suffering from quartan or tertian fever. Priests who say Mass. Shows. Various orders of monks. The prohibition of lawful marriages. Octaves. The bones of saints. Manifold orders of the cross. Kissing and adoration of the cross. Holy oil. The kiss of peace and the earnest. The theatrical acting out of the passion of Christ. The choice of a certain patron, to whom one flees in all needs. Purgatory. Pilgrimages to religious places and statues of the saints. Religious processions. The Lenten cloth. Tumultuous prayers, which are made at morning time with a solemn uproar at the sepulchre of the Lord. The Pater noster, that is, prayer beads, by which prayers are counted to God, the Creed and the Ave Maria. Blessings of cakes. Processions and pilgrimages undertaken for religion, which are made on the feast of St Mark and in Rogation week. Responsories. Rosaries. Consecrated palm branches. The golden rose. Veneration of the relics of the saints. Various societies, such as of Jesus and of the blessed Virgin, etc. Statues of the saints. Subdeacons. Consecrated salt. Hail Queen. Satisfactions, or amends for sins. The noise made with rattles or wooden instruments in the churches on the day of the Lord's Parasceve. A wooden statue of Christ, which is drawn by a rope to the upper part of the church, after the offerings and fire are cast down, and water is poured out from on high on the day of the Lord's Ascension. In some places a monk or little priest is carried up on high in a wooden machine.

units.la: Sepulcrum Domini quod singulis annis die mortis Christi erigitur.
units.tr: The sepulchre of the Lord, which is erected every year on the day of Christ's death.

units.la: Templorum dedicationes. Tonsorista[?]. Tonsiones & rasurae verticis.
units.tr: Dedications of churches. Tonsures. Shavings and shaving of the crown.

units.la: Tabulæ pictæ. Thuribula. Thymiamata & odorata. Tusio pectoris ad elevationem hostiæ & aliàs inter orandum.
units.tr: Painted tables. Censers. Incense and perfumes. Beating of the breast at the elevation of the host, and at other times while praying.

units.la: Unctio extrema seu infirmorum.
units.tr: Extreme unction, or anointing of the sick.

units.la: Unctio infantum in baptismo, & adultorum in confirmatione.
units.tr: Anointing of infants in baptism, and of adults in confirmation.

units.la: Vigiliæ pro defunctis. Vestes religiosæ & consecratæ quæ induta sanctimoniam singularem afferant. Vexilla.
units.tr: Vigils for the dead. Religious and consecrated vestments which, once put on, bring singular holiness. Banners.

units.la: Xenia sacrificulis & Monachis quotannis distribuenda.
units.tr: Gifts to be distributed yearly to little priests and monks.

units.la: Sed quis omnes ineptissimas traditiones Papisticas enumeret? Ista hoc tempore exempli gratiâ sufficiant.
units.tr: But who could list all the most absurd Papistical traditions? Let these suffice for now as examples.

units.la: LXVI.
units.tr: LXVI.

units.la: Contra has & similes traditiones nobis est certamen, non contra sanctas & utiles Ecclesiæ constitutiones, quæ vel ad disciplinam vel honestatem vel pacem conservandæ faciunt.
units.tr: Our struggle is against these and similar traditions, not against the holy and useful constitutions of the Church, which serve either for discipline, decency or the preservation of peace.

units.la: LXVII.
units.tr: LXVII.

units.la: Attamen si traditiones quædam sunt de rebus indifferentibus per se, ea possunt ad tempus ἁπλῶς[?] sine superstitione observari propter fratres infirmos.
units.tr: Nevertheless, if some traditions concern things indifferent in themselves, these may for a time be observed simply [άπλῶς] without superstition, on account of weak brothers.

units.la: LXIIX.
units.tr: LXVIII.

units.la: Cujusmodi sunt, ne palam die Veneris carnibus vescantur; aut feriis in publico laborent, aut simile quidpiam.
units.tr: Such are: not to eat meat openly on Friday; or to work publicly on holy days; or something similar.

units.la: LXIX.
units.tr: LXIX.

units.la: Hæc enim tametsi seposita[?] superstitione, indifferentia per se sint: ubi tamen accedit fratrum offensio, sine delicto admitti nequeunt, cum eorum conscientiam gravissimè vulnerent.
units.tr: For these things, although in themselves indifferent when set apart from superstition, cannot be admitted without sin once the offence of the brethren comes in, since they grievously wound their conscience.

units.la: LXX.
units.tr: LXX.

units.la: Idem propositum fuit Apostolis, ut offensionum materiâ tollerent, manducatione idolothytorum, suffocati & sanguinis fidelibus ex gentibus conversis interdixerunt.
units.tr: The Apostles had the same aim, that they might remove the matter of offence, and forbade the faithful from the Gentiles who had been converted to eat things sacrificed to idols, and what was strangled and blood.

units.la: LXXI
units.tr: LXXI

units.la: Prudentia igitur spiritualis opus est, in observatione ejusmodi traditionum.
units.tr: Spiritual prudence is therefore needed in the observance of such traditions.

units.la: LXXII.
units.tr: LXXII.

units.la: Nulla vero humanæ traditiones divinis sunt exæquandæ.
units.tr: Indeed, human traditions must not be equated with divine ones.

units.la: LXXIII.
units.tr: LXXIII.

units.la: Quapropter impium esse asserimus Concilij Tridentini decretum Sess. 4. promulgatum, quo dicitur: quòd Synodus traditiones ipsas (intellige Papisticas) tum ad fidem, tum ad mores pertinentes, tanquam vel oretenus à Christo vel à Spiritu sancto dictatas & continua successione in Ecclesia Catholica conservatas, pari pietatis affectu ac reverentia suscipit & veneratur.
units.tr: Therefore we assert that the decree of the Council of Trent, promulgated in Session 4, is impious, in which it is said: that the Synod receives and venerates with equal affection of piety and reverence the traditions themselves (understand the Papistical ones), those pertaining both to faith and to morals, as dictated either by Christ by word of mouth or by the Holy Spirit, and preserved by continuous succession in the Catholic Church.

units.la: LXXIV.
units.tr: LXXIV.

units.la: Et huic decreto opponimus illud Pauli Apostoli Gal.3. 8. 9.
units.tr: And against this decree we set that saying of the Apostle Paul, Gal. 3. 8. 9.

units.la: Etiamsi nos, aut Angelus é cœlo euangelizet vobis præter id quod vobis euãgelizavimus, anathema esto. Vt ante diximus, etiam nunc iterum dico, si quis vobis euangelizaverit præter id quod accepistis, anathema esto.
units.tr: Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach the gospel to you other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed. As we said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches the gospel to you other than what you have received, let him be accursed.

units.la: LXXV.
units.tr: LXXV.

units.la: Quid de traditionibus sit statuendum, ex hactenus dictis liquet: unde consequitur, ex quatuor illis modis probandi dogmata fidei, quos Bellarminus recenset Disputationum Tomo 1. Sexta Cotrov. Generali, quæ est de Purgatorio, lib. 1. cap. undec. duos tantum primos modos, vid. 1. per expressa Scriptura testimonia cum Ecclesiæ declaratione, sed (quod addendum est) fidei ἀναλόγως petita ex ipsa Scriptura Canonica, non co-ficta[?] extra Scriptura. 2. per evidentem deductionem ex iis, quæ habentur expressè in Scriptura: hos, inquam, duos modos tantum certos & recipiendos esse.
units.tr: What must be determined about traditions is clear from what has been said so far. From this it follows that of those four modes of proving the dogmas of faith which Bellarmine lists in Disputations, Volume 1, the sixth general controversy, which concerns Purgatory, book 1, chapter 11, only the first two modes are to be recognised: namely, (1) through express testimonies of Scripture together with the declaration of the Church, but (what must be added) the articles of faith drawn proportionately from Canonical Scripture itself, not invented outside Scripture; (2) through evident deduction from those things which are expressly contained in Scripture. These two modes, I say, alone are certain and to be received.

units.la: LXXVI.
units.tr: LXXVI.

units.la: Reliquos autè duos modos, nempe, per traditiones nō scriptas & per evidentem deductionem ex traditionibus non scriptis, esse incertos, ac repudiandos.
units.tr: The remaining two modes, namely through unwritten traditions and through evident deduction from unwritten traditions, are uncertain and to be rejected.

units.la: DOMINO IESU CHRISTO SERVATORI nostro sit gloria in sempiternum ævum.
units.tr: To the Lord Jesus Christ, our Saviour, be glory for ever and ever.

units.la: PRECATIO AD CHRISTVM.
units.tr: PRAYER TO CHRIST.

units.la: CHRISTE tuū defende gregē, quem Papa scelestus Fraudibus & bellis undiq; ferme petit. Et quem diversis nunc Turca fatigat in oris, Qui nulli parcens, sanguine cuncta replet. Demonstra roburq; tuum, curamq; tuorum, Sentiat atq; iras hostis uterq; tuas. Ne nostri sceleris, sed fœderis illius almi sis memor & populū protege, CHRISTE, tuū.
units.tr: CHRIST, defend your flock, which the wicked Pope attacks almost everywhere with frauds and wars, and which the Turk now harasses in various lands, sparing no one and filling everything with blood. Show your strength and your care for your own, and let both enemies feel your wrath. Remember not our wickedness but that kindly covenant, and protect your people, CHRIST.
